passages.text: Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by dysfunction of the endosomal-lysosomal system (ELS). <sentence_start/>Four shared neurodegenerative mechanisms across ALS, PD and AD are regulated by the ELS, namely proteostasis and related protein misfolding, mitochondrial function, neurotransmission and neuroinflammation. <sentence_start/>These mechanisms are interconnected, contributing to neurodegeneration in a “snowball” manner. <sentence_start/>The retromer, a multimeric, evolutionarily conserved protein complex involved in intracellular protein trafficking, is at the crossroad of these neurodegenerative processes. <sentence_start/>This narrative review focuses on exploring the retromer structure, function as a master regulator of the ELS, and how this impacts proteostasis, mitochondrial biogenesis and homeostasis, neurotransmission and neuroinflammation across neurodegenerative diseases. <sentence_start/>We explore how alterations in retromer function can play an important role in neurodegeneration and discuss the impact of genetic and pharmacological manipulations of VPS35, one of the main retromer subunits. <sentence_start/>In vitro and in vivo studies have identified that the retromer enhances the activity of protein degradation pathways via the ELS, namely macroautophagy, chaperone-mediated autophagy, and the ELS itself, with concomitant reduction in misfolded protein levels. <sentence_start/>Also, in some model systems, when the retromer role is enhanced or restored, mitochondrial function is rescued, dysfunctional neurotransmission is restored, and the damaging effects of neuroinflammation are dampened. <sentence_start/>Lastly, we highlight the role of a novel pharmacological class of agents that enhance retromer function as a strategy for potentially slowing the progression of these neurodegenerative diseases in in vivo models of PD and ALS. <sentence_start/>We discuss the challenges in targeting the retromer, current limitations and potential off-target effects of retromer enhancement. <sentence_start/>Overall, the retromer regulates shared mechanisms across neurodegenerative diseases and retromer enhancers could represent a novel disease-modifying strategy in AD, PD and ALS.

This review analyzes the retromer complex-mediated modulation of the endosomal-lysosomal system (ELS) in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and explores how this affects their pathophysiology. <sentence_start/>As such, this review provides a description of the retromer complex structure and assembly process and AD, PD and ALS pathophysiology. <sentence_start/>This is followed by an analysis of the pathophysiology of the endosomal-lysosomal system (ELS) in health and neurodegenerative diseases, the retromer’s role in it and a detailed analysis of the ELS-mediated retromer role in regulating cellular proteostasis, mitochondrial function, neurotransmission and neuroinflammation in AD, PD and ALS. <sentence_start/>This review ends with a discussion of the potential role of the retromer as a therapeutic target and challenges of targeting the retromer with small molecules.

The retromer is an evolutionarily conserved multimeric complex originally identified in the budding yeast <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces cerevisiae</italic> by Seaman and colleagues [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.142.3.665" pmid="9700157" pmcid="PMC2148169" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In yeasts, the retromer is a stable heteropentamer composed of five distinct proteins encoded by the vacuole protein sorting (<italic toggle="yes">VPS</italic>) genes, i.e. <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">VPS26</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">VPS29</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">VPS5</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">VPS17</italic> [<citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb1103" pmid="16732284" pmcid="PMC1584284" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The heterotrimer Vps35/Vps26/Vps29 recruits the heterodimer Vps5/Vps17 sequentially [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.142.3.665" pmid="9700157" pmcid="PMC2148169" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The process of retromer-mediated vesicle formation at the endosome starts with the binding of Vps35 to the aromatic tail of transmembrane endosomal proteins such as Vps10 or Kex2p [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.142.3.665" pmid="9700157" pmcid="PMC2148169" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Next, Vps29 is recruited and activates Vps35, which clusters with the cargo protein. <sentence_start/>This is the signal that recruits the Vps5/Vps17 heterodimer [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.142.3.665" pmid="9700157" pmcid="PMC2148169" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Vps5 binds both Vps29 and Vps35 subunits through its unstructured N-terminal domain [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58846-8" pmid="40234461" pmcid="PMC12000511" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The final structure of the retromer assembled on the endosomal membrane has been characterized in the thermophilic ascomycete <italic toggle="yes">Chaetomium thermophilum</italic> via cryo-electron tomography [<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2005.10.012" pmid="16243015" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Each one of two copies of the heterotrimer Vps35/Vps26/Vps29 sits on a membrane-bound Vps5 interface and forms a dimeric arch [<citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.str.2020.03.009" pmid="32268076" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Vps26 forms the “foot” between each Vps35 “leg” and Vps5 [<citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.str.2020.03.009" pmid="32268076" count="1">5</citation>].

In mammals, the retromer has a 150-kD core heterotrimer composed of VPS26, VPS35, and VPS29 (formerly called the cargo-selection complex, CSC), which is responsible for binding transmembrane cargo proteins (Fig. 1) [<citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jbc.2022.102523" pmid="36174678" pmcid="PMC9636581" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>With its α-solenoid structure, VPS35 provides a flexible platform for binding VPS26 at its N-terminus and VPS29 at its C-terminus [<citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature06216" pmid="17891154" pmcid="PMC2377034" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The stability of the heterotrimer depends on VPS35, and hence, the modulation of this protein is commonly used to study retromer function. <sentence_start/>In mammals, VPS26 exists in two isoforms, VPS26A and VPS26B, whereas VPS29 has three isoforms, VPS29A, VPS29B and VPS29C [<citation rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0854.2011.01284.x" pmid="21920005" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2501111122" pmid="40587794" pmcid="PMC12260524" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer binds a dimer of different sorting nexin (SNX) proteins, previously called the tubulation module, as SNXs drive tubule formation [<citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jbc.2022.102523" pmid="36174678" pmcid="PMC9636581" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, the SNX family of proteins serves as the scaffold for the retromer, which lacks a domain capable of binding membrane phospholipids (Fig. 1) [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.00090" pmid="12244127" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The SNX family of proteins encompasses SNX with a Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domain that binds phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) and SNXs without a BAR domain (e.g. SNX3, SNX27) capable of interacting with PI3P through different domains (e.g. phox-homolog domain for SNX3) [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.00090" pmid="12244127" count="1">10</citation>-<citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrm2427" pmid="18523436" count="1">12</citation>].

Retromer structure and its central role in neurodegeneration. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) The mammalian retromer is composed of two copies of VPS35 and VPS29 dimers that form an arch on the VPS26 interface, with VPS26 forming the ‘‘foot’’ between each VPS35 ‘‘leg’’. <sentence_start/>With its α-solenoid structure, VPS35 binds VPS26 at its N-terminus and Vps29 at its C-terminus. <sentence_start/>Sorting nexins are the retromer subunits that bind to membrane phospholipids. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Via modulation of the endosomal-lysosomal system, the retromer regulates cellular proteostasis, mitochondrial function, neurotransmission and neuroinflammation, whose dysfunction is involved in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative conditions

The retromer can bind the heterodimer composed of a combination of SNX1 or SNX2 with SNX5, SNX6, SNX3 and the metazoan-specific SNX27 [<citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jbc.2022.102523" pmid="36174678" pmcid="PMC9636581" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX1/2 is a mammalian homolog of the yeast Vps5, whereas SNX5/6 is the homolog of the yeast Vps17 [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1091/mbc.E02-03-0145" pmid="12388759" pmcid="PMC129968" count="1">13</citation>-<citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2022.105768" pmid="35588987" pmcid="PMC9233057" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The heterodimeric complex composed of a combination of SNX1 or SNX2 with SNX5, SNX6 or SNX32 is also known as the endosomal sorting complex for promoting exit 1 (ESCPE-1), a complex distinct from the retromer with the ability to bind its own cargo [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41556-019-0393-3" pmid="31576058" pmcid="PMC6778059" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ESCPE-1 is involved in the sorting of over sixty transmembrane protein cargoes in the ELS [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41556-019-0393-3" pmid="31576058" pmcid="PMC6778059" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201702137" pmid="28935632" pmcid="PMC5674888" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ESCPE-1 cargoes are rescued from the early endosome (EE) and late endosome (LE) to the <italic toggle="yes">trans</italic>-Golgi network (TGN) and the plasma membrane [<citation rid="CR18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-023-01014-7" pmid="37322239" pmcid="PMC10352136" count="1">18</citation>, <citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/tra.12885" pmid="37089068" pmcid="PMC10768393" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a handover model, SNX27 associates with the retromer and cargo proteins captured by the SNX27-retromer are transferred to ESCPE-1 to promote endosome-to-plasma membrane recycling [<citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3001601" pmid="35417450" pmcid="PMC9038204" count="1">20</citation>].

The nexin dimer is necessary but not sufficient to recruit the retromer on the endosomal membrane because of their weak interaction, so this requires a second key protein, the small guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase) RAB7a [<citation rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200804048" pmid="18981234" pmcid="PMC2575791" count="1">21</citation>, <citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tibs.2020.12.009" pmid="33526371" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The importance of RAB7a is confirmed by studies showing that the GTPase-activating protein TBC1D5 (TBC1 domain family member 5), by deactivating RAB7a, inhibits the retromer recruitment process [<citation rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.048686" pmid="19531583" pmcid="PMC2704877" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.217398" pmcid="PMC6031384" pmid="29777037" count="1">24</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, RAB7a localization is maintained by both the retromer and TBC1D5. <sentence_start/>In the absence of either TBC1D5, VPS35 or VPS29, RAB7a activity state and localization are no longer properly controlled [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.201797128" pmid="29158324" pmcid="PMC5770787" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer is recruited to the endosomal surface by RAB7a and nexins and starts tubule formation by orchestrating the SNX proteins’ distribution on the endosomal membrane [<citation rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200804048" pmid="18981234" pmcid="PMC2575791" count="1">21</citation>, <citation rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/jcs.048686" pmid="19531583" pmcid="PMC2704877" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnsyn.2018.00037" pmid="30405388" pmcid="PMC6207580" count="1">26</citation>].

The process of endosomal tubulation and scission is facilitated by the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and SCAR homolog (WASH) complex [<citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.devcel.2009.09.010" pmid="19922875" count="1">27</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This multimeric structure interacts with the retromer via the FAM21 (family with sequence similarity 21) tail of the protein WASH, with the binding site located on VPS35 and VPS29 [<citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2405041121" pmid="39116126" pmcid="PMC11331091" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/pro.4980" pmid="38607248" pmcid="PMC11010949" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, FAM21 also interacts with SNX27 and SNX1 [<citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2405041121" pmid="39116126" pmcid="PMC11331091" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24643499" doi="10.1242/jcs.144659" pmcid="PMC4004978" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The SNX1 interaction happens via the protein RME8, and loss of this protein leads to impairment in the SNX1 association with the endosomal membrane and with the formation of branched endosomal tubules [<citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24643499" doi="10.1242/jcs.144659" pmcid="PMC4004978" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>After the binding is achieved, additional actors take part in the polymerization of the actin network around the endosomal tubules, which contributes to endosomal tubulation and scission [<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2009.10.019" pmid="19835875" count="1">31</citation>].

The term neurodegenerative disease encompasses a wide range of pathologies impacting the peripheral and central nervous system, characterized by a progressive loss of neurons and altered function of glial cells. <sentence_start/>In this review, we focus on AD, PD, and ALS.

<italic toggle="yes">Alzheimer’s disease:</italic> AD is the most common neurodegenerative disease in the United States [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/B978-0-12-804766-8.00013-3" pmid="31753135" count="1">32</citation>] and the most common form of dementia worldwide in the older population [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2174/1567205014666170203125942" pmid="28164766" pmcid="PMC5684784" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>AD pathogenesis starts with the internalization of the 770 amino acid transmembrane protein amyloid precursor protein (APP) from the cell surface to early endosomes. <sentence_start/>APP undergoes a sequential cut first by beta-site amyloid precursor protein cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1, also known as β-secretases), releasing soluble APP β (sAPPβ) and with the C99 residue remaining in the endosomal membrane. <sentence_start/>As the second step, γ-secretases cleave C99 in the amyloid-β (Aβ) fibrillary protein and the amyloid precursor intracellular domain (AICD) [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0854.2012.01332.x" pmid="22269004" count="1">34</citation>] (Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>Aβ compromises synaptic signaling, triggers microglial activation via Aβ oligomers, and triggers the conversion of the microtubule-associated protein tau from a normal to a toxic state [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1072994" pmid="12130773" count="1">35</citation>-<citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamaneurol.2013.5847" pmid="24493463" pmcid="PMC12908160" count="1">37</citation>].

Retromer role in amyloid precursor protein (APP) processing in Alzheimer’s disease. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) APP internalization: APP is internalized from the cell surface to the early endosomes via a clathrin-mediated mechanism. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Amyloidogenic pathway: APP undergoes a sequential cut first by β-secretases, releasing soluble APP β (sAPP β) and with the C99 residue remaining in the endosomal membrane. <sentence_start/>As the second step, γ-secretases cleave C99 in the Aβ fibrillary protein and the amyloid precursor intracellular domain (AICD). <sentence_start/>(<bold>C</bold>) APP trafficking: APP circulates between the trans-Golgi (TGN) network, early endosome and plasma membrane, or late endosome and lysosome. <sentence_start/>SORL1, via interaction with Vps26b, carries APP from endosomal compartments to the (i) TGN or (ii) plasma membrane, evading the intracellular amyloidogenic pathway; (iii) Endosomal defects associated with AD promote APP enzymatic processing by β-secretases, initiating the amyloidogenic pathway; (iv) Aβ and APP clearance: The retromer modulates the clearance of Aβ via the distribution of the cathepsin-carrying protein CI-MPR to late endosomes and lysosomes. <sentence_start/>Created in

<italic toggle="yes">Parkinson’s disease:</italic> PD is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 1% of people over 65 and 4.3% of those older than 85 [<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.26424" pmid="26474316" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Much of the motor symptoms, which are the basis of the clinical diagnosis of PD [<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.26424" pmid="26474316" count="1">38</citation>], are attributed to the preferential loss of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the <italic toggle="yes">substantia nigra</italic> (SN), resulting in degeneration of the nigrostriatal tract and dopamine deficiency [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/PL00007758" pmid="10991663" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A convincing set of data from genetic, animal models, and biochemical studies supports the view that accumulation and aggregation of the protein α-synuclein (αS) in DA neurons may represent a key pathogenic event for PD (Fig. 3) [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrn3406" pmid="23254192" pmcid="PMC4295774" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>αS is a protein usually present in the cytoplasm of neurons whose native conformation and related PD pathogenetic mechanisms are a matter of debate. <sentence_start/>Initial analysis revealed native αS as a 14 KDa unfolded monomer, with an imbalance between the αS rate of synthesis and clearance resulting in abnormal αS concentrations that might push the formation and accumulation of toxic oligomeric and fibrillar species [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrn3406" pmid="23254192" pmcid="PMC4295774" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Further studies highlighted the 58 kDa folded tetramer with an α-helical structure as the native αS form, and it has been proposed that destabilization of the tetramer precedes the αS misfolding and aggregation in toxic oligomeric and fibrillar species [<citation rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature10324" pmid="21841800" pmcid="PMC3166366" count="1">41</citation>-<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1113260108" pmid="22006323" pmcid="PMC3203798" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The αS fibrils release prefibrillar oligomers, which, due to solvent-exposed hydrophobic functional groups, are capable of permeabilizing neuronal membranes, leading to cellular insults [<citation rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-021-21937-3" pmid="33753734" pmcid="PMC7985515" count="1">44</citation>].

Retromer role in α-Synuclein degradation in Parkinson’s disease. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Endosomal-lysosomal system: Cathepsin D (CTSD) and cathepsin L (CTSL) are involved in the lysosomal degradation of α-Synuclein. <sentence_start/>Sortilin (not depicted) and CI-MPR are involved in the sorting of lysosomal hydrolases. <sentence_start/>The retromer regulates the sorting of CI-MPR between the trans-Golgi network, early, late endosomes, and lysosomes. <sentence_start/>The retromer controls the localization of RAB5 and RAB7, important mediators of the ELS. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): Soluble α-Synuclein carries the KFERQ recognition motif recognized by the chaperone proteins Heat Shock Cognate 70 (HSC70), which sorts the substrate to Lysosomal-Associated Membrane Protein 2 A (LAMP2A). <sentence_start/>VPS35 regulates LAMP2A transport to and from the lysosome, and retromer enhancement increases levels of HSC70 and LAMP2A. (<bold>C</bold>) Macroautophagy: Insoluble α-Synuclein is degraded via macroautophagy. <sentence_start/>VPS35 governs macroautophagy by controlling the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog (WASH) complex’s sorting and recycling by interacting directly with one of its subunits, the protein FAM21, and by modulating p62 and LC3-II levels. <sentence_start/>Created in

<italic toggle="yes">Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis:</italic> ALS is a motor neuron disease characterized by the rapid progression of upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, resulting in progressive muscle weakness and eventually death [<citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13311-014-0331-9" pmid="25582382" pmcid="PMC4404434" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The pathogenesis of ALS is only partially understood and partially based on pre-clinical data from familial forms of ALS. <sentence_start/>The superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) gene mutation is the second most common cause of hereditary forms of ALS, accounting for ~ 20% of familial ALS cases [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMra1603471" pmid="28700839" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Mutant SOD1 protein tends to misfold, with subsequent formation of aggregates that lead to motoneuron injury and death (Fig. 4) [<citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1312245111" pmid="24550511" pmcid="PMC3948312" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Mutations in transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (<italic toggle="yes">TDP-43</italic>), a gene for RNA-binding proteins, are also involved in familial ALS [<citation rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bmb/ldw026" pmid="27450455" count="1">48</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Mutated TDP-43 is found primarily in the cytoplasm instead of the nucleus, causing neurodegeneration (Fig. 4) [<citation rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bmb/ldw026" pmid="27450455" count="1">48</citation>]. <sentence_start/>TDP-43 mutations lead to misfolding and aggregation (Fig. 4) [<citation rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M114.561704" pmid="24825905" pmcid="PMC4081952" count="1">49</citation>]. <sentence_start/>TDP-43 aggregates sequester the normal function of TDP-43, but these aggregates also actively cause splicing dysregulation, increases in DNA damage, transcriptome-wide changes, and disruption of oxidative stress response [<citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-020-00397-1" pmid="32799899" pmcid="PMC7429473" count="1">50</citation>, <citation rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2020.105050" pmid="32800996" count="1">51</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Possible mechanisms described in ALS are oxidative stress, glutamate excitotoxicity, mitochondrial and proteasomal dysfunctions, altered synaptic function, disturbed axonal transport, and neuroinflammation [<citation rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cells12111523" pmcid="PMC10252394" pmid="37296644" count="1">52</citation>, <citation rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37283936" doi="10.17879/freeneuropathology-2023-4682" pmcid="PMC10209858" count="1">53</citation>].

Retromer role in motor neurons. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Healthy motor neurons: (i) TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) and Superoxide Dismutase 1 (SOD1) maintain their physiological nuclear and cytosolic localization, respectively, without significant misfolding and aggregating; (ii) NIMA-related Kinase 1 (NEK1) regulates retromer-mediated endosomal trafficking by phosphorylating VPS26B; (iii) the retromer, via the interaction with Cation-Independent Mannose Phosphate Receptor (CI-MPR) which carries cathepsins, coordinates cathepsins transport to the lysosomes where they catabolize polypeptides in peptides; (iv) retromer facilitates the Glutamate Receptor Subunit A1 (GluA1, or GluR1) recycling to the synaptic membrane in the interface motor neuron-interneuron. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis motor neurons have decreased levels of retromer and NEK2: (i) TDP-43 mis-localizes to the cytosol, (ii) TDP-43 and SOD-1 misfold and form misfolded protein aggregates, (iii) a reduced amount of cathepsins is carried to the lysosomes, with consequent impaired enzymatic proteolysis, (iv) decreased levels of VPS35 limit GluA1 recycling on the synaptic membrane. <sentence_start/>Created in
Endosomal-lysosomal system dysfunction is the culprit of neurodegenerative diseases

AD, PD, ALS are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by progressive neuronal loss in selective central nervous system regions, namely the medial temporal lobe with hippocampal involvement, the lateral region of the parietal, temporal and frontal lobes in AD, the SN <italic toggle="yes">pars compacta</italic> in PD, the anterior horns of the spinal cord with lower motor neurons and the corticospinal tracts in ALS [<citation rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep46263" pmid="28417965" pmcid="PMC5394684" count="1">54</citation>-<citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/cshperspect.a024117" pmcid="PMC5538408" pmid="28003278" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Despite the degeneration of different central nervous system (CNS) areas and neuronal types, similar pathophysiological mechanisms may ignite the cascade of cellular changes that lead to neuronal loss. <sentence_start/>A key pathophysiological mechanism that has been the focus of recent research on PD, AD and ALS includes endolysosomal trafficking and vesicle-mediated protein sorting [<citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40035-020-00221-2" pmid="33239064" pmcid="PMC7689983" count="1">58</citation>-<citation rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1098/rsob.180138" pmcid="PMC6170506" pmid="30185603" count="1">60</citation>].

The ELS is an intracellular membrane-enclosed system responsible for the trafficking of intracellular proteins, glycoproteins, and protein-bound lipid cargoes that play a critical role in maintaining cellular homeostasis [<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40035-015-0041-1" pmid="26448863" pmcid="PMC4596472" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It is composed of EE, LE, lysosomes and recycling endosomes [<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40035-015-0041-1" pmid="26448863" pmcid="PMC4596472" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Molecular sorting along the ELS is regulated by the RAB proteins, a family of small GTPases [<citation rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/cshperspect.a022616" pmid="25341920" pmcid="PMC4413231" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>After internalization via clathrin-dependent mechanisms, among others, cargo proteins reach the EE under the modulation of RAB5, a marker of EE [<citation rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0092-8674(91)90316-q" pmid="1900457" count="1">63</citation>]. <sentence_start/>EE is a major hub, from which proteins can move to different destinations. <sentence_start/>The sorting to the plasma membrane or extracellular space via recycling endosomes is mediated by the retromer and involves RAB4 and RAB11 [<citation rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pneurobio.2011.10.002" pmid="22037413" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>If the delivery from the EE is to the LE, there is a switch from RAB5 to RAB7 [<citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2010.03.011" pmid="20434987" count="1">65</citation>]. <sentence_start/>LEs fuse with lysosomes, where cargo proteins are degraded by lysosomal hydrolases [<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40035-015-0041-1" pmid="26448863" pmcid="PMC4596472" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This trafficking from EE to LE to lysosomes is mediated by the endosomal complex required for transport (or ESCRT) [<citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature07961" pmid="19325624" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ESCRT recognizes ubiquitinated proteins, and the sorting process is ubiquitin-dependent [<citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature07961" pmid="19325624" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Lastly, cargoes are trafficked from the EE to the TGN via the retromer. <sentence_start/>In fact, the term “retromer” refers to the first function discovered for this complex, namely the vesicular transport of transmembrane protein cargoes from the early endosome to the <italic toggle="yes">trans</italic>-Golgi network [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.142.3.665" pmid="9700157" pmcid="PMC2148169" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer is also involved in endosomal protein trafficking from mitochondria to peroxisomes or lysosomes via mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs). <sentence_start/>These vesicular carriers transport mitochondrial proteins and lipids to other intracellular organelles (Fig. 1) [<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2010.05.066" pmid="20619655" count="1">67</citation>, <citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23148298" doi="10.1242/jcs.103440" pmcid="PMC3517092" count="1">68</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Protein cargoes recycling from the endosomes to the plasma membrane are mediated by the handoff mechanisms from the retromer: SNX27 to the ESCP-1 complex, or by the interaction between the retriever complex and the COMMD/CCDC22/CCDC93 (CCC) complex [<citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3001601" pmid="35417450" pmcid="PMC9038204" count="1">20</citation>, <citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-023-01184-4" pmid="38062209" pmcid="PMC11260360" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retriever complex is a trimeric paralog of the retromer composed of the proteins VPS35 endosomal protein-sorting factor-like protein (VPS35L), VPS26C and VPS29 [<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-023-01184-4" pmid="38062209" pmcid="PMC11260360" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The CCC complex comprises the coiled-coil domain-containing (CCDC)22, CCDC93 and copper metabolism domain-containing (COMMD) proteins [<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-023-01184-4" pmid="38062209" pmcid="PMC11260360" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retriever complex associated with SNX17 and couples to CCC and WASH complex to promote cell surface recycling [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb3610" pmid="28892079" pmcid="PMC5790113" count="1">70</citation>].

Aging affects the ELS functionality. <sentence_start/>Age-related oxidative stress increases the amount of oxidized proteins within lysosomes, which impairs lysosomal activity by compromising the functionality of membrane organelles and leading to intralysosomal protein overload [<citation rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2012.06.005" pmid="22840404" pmcid="PMC3408590" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additionally, endolysosomes increase in size and number due to acidification defects and aberrantly accumulate near synapses in aged neurons and brains [<citation rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/tra.12889" pmid="37218497" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Aging is also the primary risk factor for most neurodegenerative diseases [<citation rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41582-019-0244-7" pmid="31501588" count="1">73</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence, it is unsurprising that an aged and dysfunctional ELS remains central in the processes of neurodegeneration. <sentence_start/>In AD postmortem brains, a cytopathologic hallmark of the disease is abnormal enlargement of early endosomes [<citation rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tins.2017.08.003" pmid="28962801" pmcid="PMC5654621" count="1">74</citation>, <citation rid="CR75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnins.2017.00702" pmid="29311783" pmcid="PMC5733017" count="1">75</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This finding can be related to the dysfunction of the endosomal system, with an amyloid-independent traffic jam resulting in enlarged and dysfunctional endosomes, which subsequently mediates amyloid, tau, synaptic and microglia pathology [<citation rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tins.2017.08.003" pmid="28962801" pmcid="PMC5654621" count="1">74</citation>-<citation rid="CR76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/scitranslmed.abb1717" pmcid="PMC8025181" pmid="33268506" count="1">76</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In autopsy of sporadic PD brains, early endosomes maturation and trafficking are disrupted, lysosomes are changed in shape and size with electron microscopy highlighting swollen and fragmented lysosomes [<citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2009.05.023" pmid="19505575" count="1">77</citation>-<citation rid="CR79" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2019.104626" pmid="31618685" pmcid="PMC7345850" count="1">79</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Mutations in several genes encoding ELS proteins, including VPS35, cause familial forms of PD. <sentence_start/>For example, glucocebrebrosidase (<italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic>) gene mutation leads to early-onset PD. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> encodes for a lysosomal enzyme and its mutation leads to enlarged lysosomes, with increased electron-dense material, suggesting that their contents are not cleared appropriately [<citation rid="CR80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.stemcr.2016.01.013" pmcid="PMC4788783" pmid="26905200" count="1">80</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, different authors argue that the ELS dysfunction drives αS pathology [<citation rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature20414" pmid="27830778" count="1">81</citation>, <citation rid="CR82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awy147" pmcid="PMC6061679" pmid="29860491" count="1">82</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Aberrant and enlarged endosomes are also observed in sporadic ALS tissues [<citation rid="CR83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2202-12-24" pmid="21385376" pmcid="PMC3058068" count="1">83</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The classic ALS mouse model, the <italic toggle="yes">wobbler</italic> mouse, has a partial loss-of-function mutation in the <italic toggle="yes">Vps54</italic> gene, a component of the Golgi-associated retrograde protein (GARP) complex, which recycles cargoes from the LE to the TGN [<citation rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng1661" pmid="16244655" count="1">84</citation>, <citation rid="CR85" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tcb.2010.11.003" pmid="21183348" pmcid="PMC3073588" count="1">85</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Lastly, in ALS pre-clinical models, TDP-43 accumulation was found to be a downstream event secondary to the disruption of the endolysosomal pathway [<citation rid="CR86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tins.2023.09.004" pmid="37827960" pmcid="PMC10841821" count="1">86</citation>].

A dysfunctional ELS is associated with four mechanisms known to trigger neurobiological degenerative processes: (i) proteostasis with protein misfolding and aggregation, (ii) dysfunction of mitochondria biogenesis and homeostasis, (iii) neurotransmission and (iv) neuroinflammation (Fig. 1) [<citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40035-020-00221-2" pmid="33239064" pmcid="PMC7689983" count="1">58</citation>-<citation rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1098/rsob.180138" pmcid="PMC6170506" pmid="30185603" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These mechanisms have been identified as potentially relevant in ALS, PD and AD in a 2025 large-scale high-throughput proteomic study led by the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium, highlighting converging biological pathways across neurodegenerative diseases centered around the ELS [<citation rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-025-03834-0" pmcid="PMC12353841" pmid="40665048" count="1">87</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, a dysfunctional ELS represents an initial driving force upstream of these shared mechanisms. <sentence_start/>As a subsequent step, these initial dysfunctional pathogenic processes affect one another and themselves in a “snowball” effect, leading to neurodegeneration.
The retromer is at the crossroads of neurodegenerative diseases

In this context, an emerging role in neurodegeneration has been identified for the retromer complex. <sentence_start/>The retromer complex plays a role in neuron development and survival, as demonstrated by a mouse model in which pan-neuronal deletion of VPS35 leads to early post-natal lethality and by another mouse model in which homozygous deletion of <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> leads to early embryonic lethality [<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/braincomms/fcab208" pmcid="PMC8445400" pmid="34704029" count="1">88</citation>, <citation rid="CR89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201105109" pmid="22105352" pmcid="PMC3257571" count="1">89</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Correlative analysis between RNA-Seq and the whole cell proteome from <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> knock-out (KO) cell lines has revealed disease signatures typical of PD, AD and ALS, among others [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To follow, we discuss the genetic data linking the retromer to AD, PD, and ALS.

<italic toggle="yes">AD, retromer and genetics: </italic>The retromer protein VPS35 is deficient in vulnerable regions in AD brains [<citation rid="CR91" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ana.20667" pmid="16315276" count="1">91</citation>], and a rare <italic toggle="yes">de novo VPS35</italic> variant with missense mutation Leu625Pro has been identified in sporadic early-onset AD [<citation rid="CR92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/mp.2015.100" pmid="26194182" count="1">92</citation>], as have variants in a range of other retromer-related genes [<citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2012.04.020" pmcid="PMC3391348" pmid="22673115" count="1">93</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer subunit VPS26B was found to be enriched in the trans-entorhinal cortex of human brains and deficient in AD [<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110182" pmid="34965419" pmcid="PMC8792909" count="1">94</citation>].

Amyloid precursor-like protein 2 (APLP2) and tau were among the most significantly enriched proteins in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of <italic toggle="yes">Vps35</italic> KO mice [<citation rid="CR95" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/scitranslmed.aba6334" pmcid="PMC7901670" pmid="33239387" count="1">95</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Wen et al. have confirmed that mice with a hemizygous deletion of <italic toggle="yes">Vps35</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">Vps26</italic> heterozygote KO develop hippocampal-dependent memory and synaptic dysfunction associated with endogenous Aβ peptide accumulation [<citation rid="CR89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201105109" pmid="22105352" pmcid="PMC3257571" count="1">89</citation>, <citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0802545105" pmid="18480253" pmcid="PMC2386077" count="1">96</citation>] due to an increase in BACE1 activity [<citation rid="CR89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201105109" pmid="22105352" pmcid="PMC3257571" count="1">89</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These data suggest a retromer loss-of-function as a pathogenetic event in AD and increasing retromer levels as a potential therapeutic strategy for countering AD pathology.

<italic toggle="yes">PD, retromer and genetics: </italic><italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> is among the genes related to familial forms of PD. <sentence_start/>The most common <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> mutation, the missense mutation Asp620Asn (D620N), is responsible for an autosomal dominant form of PD that is similar to its idiopathic form [<citation rid="CR97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.06.001" pmid="21763482" pmcid="PMC3135796" count="1">97</citation>, <citation rid="CR98" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.06.008" pmid="21763483" pmcid="PMC3135812" count="1">98</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Whether this mutation leads to a VPS35 loss of function, gain of function or both is still subject to debate. <sentence_start/>Alessi et al. demonstrated that VPS35 controls the Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) activity and that the <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> mutation is associated with hyperactivation of the LRRK2 kinase and subsequent hyperphosphorylation of RAB8A, RAB10, and RAB12 [<citation rid="CR99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/BCJ20180248" pmid="29743203" pmcid="PMC5989534" count="1">99</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Also, <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> knock-in (KI) mice have been shown to have abnormal tau hyperphosphorylation, tau-positive somatodendritic pathology throughout the brain, and progressive degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, suggesting another mechanism through which <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> can lead to toxicity [<citation rid="CR100" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1814909116" pmid="30842285" pmcid="PMC6431187" count="1">100</citation>]. <sentence_start/>On the other end of the spectrum, the <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> mutation impairs synaptic function, disrupts retromer cargo protein sorting, and impairs macroautophagy, chaperone-mediated autophagy, and the ELS, and alters mitochondrial homeostasis, highlighting also a potential loss-of-function role. <sentence_start/>These potential loss-of-function mechanisms will be addressed in the next paragraphs.

<italic toggle="yes">ALS, retromer and genetics: </italic>In ALS patients, different studies demonstrated a reduction in VPS35, VPS29, VPS26A levels [<citation rid="CR101" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2023.113636" pmid="38183652" pmcid="PMC10926001" count="1">101</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence was also confirmed in transgenic mice expressing the mutant SOD1 G93A [<citation rid="CR102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2118755119" pmid="35749364" pmcid="PMC9245686" count="1">102</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Muzio et al. demonstrate a significant reduction in the retromer subunits VPS35 and VPS26 in IPSC-derived motor neurons (MNs) from ALS patients, in the ventral horn MNs from ALS post-mortem explants, and in MNs from an ALS mouse model (SOD1<sup>G93A</sup>) [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence is further strengthened by evidence of spinal cord motor neuron degeneration in conditional KO mice with selective deletion of <italic toggle="yes">Vps35</italic> in neurons [<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/braincomms/fcab208" pmcid="PMC8445400" pmid="34704029" count="1">88</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The decrease in retromer subunit levels in the ALS mouse model is prodromal to MN degeneration, raising the possibility that the retromer complex could represent a trigger for neurodegeneration [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>].
The retromer is a master regulator of the endosomal-lysosomal system

As previously described, the retromer plays a key role in cargo trafficking from the EE to the plasma membrane or the TGN, and from mitochondria to peroxisomes or lysosomes (Fig. 5). <sentence_start/>The relevance of the retromer in modulating the ELS has been demonstrated in <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> knockout (KO) H4 neuroglioma cells and mouse neurons, which revealed profound changes to the endo-lysosomal network, with hybrid and enlarged endo-lysosomal compartments loaded with undigested intraluminal material, and limited degradative capacity [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An integrated multi-omics approach in the same in vitro model revealed significant depletion of lysosomal hydrolases [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To follow, a detailed discussion of the ELS mechanisms regulated by the retromer.

Role of the retromer complex in endosomal protein trafficking and lysosomal homeostasis. <sentence_start/>Schematic representation of retromer-mediated trafficking pathways within the endolysosomal system. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Retrograde trafficking: The retromer complex, composed of the core subunits VPS35-VPS26-VPS29, is recruited to early endosomal membranes, where the VPS35 subunit mediates the recognition of selected cargoes, including the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR) and Sortilin, that are sorted from early endosomes back to the trans-Golgi network (TGN). <sentence_start/>This pathway is essential for the proper recycling of CI-MPR and Sortilin, which at the TGN subsequently regulate, through retromer-independent mechanisms, the sorting and trafficking of lysosomal hydrolases, such as cathepsin D (CTSD), through early endosome and late endosomes, ensuring their efficient delivery to lysosomes. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Endosome-to-plasma membrane recycling pathway: The retromer regulates the retrieval of surface receptors, such as the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2AR), thereby preventing their mis-sorting toward late endosomes and lysosomal degradation. <sentence_start/>β2AR is recognized by the VPS35 subunit in the early endosomes and sorted to the plasma membrane. <sentence_start/>β2AR internalization from the plasma membrane to early endosomes is a retromer-independent mechanism. <sentence_start/>Created in

<italic toggle="yes">Lysosomal hydrolase sorting: </italic> VPS35 indirectly controls lysosomal activity by transporting lysosomal hydrolase receptors, such as cation-independent 6-mannose phosphate receptor (CI-MPR) and Sortilin (Fig. 5) [<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312055" pmid="15078903" pmcid="PMC2172094" count="1">104</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These receptors are directly involved in the sorting and subsequent maturation of lysosomal hydrolases. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> KO reduces lysosomal proteolytic function because of the disrupted processing of lysosomal hydrolases, dependent on the trafficking of the CI-MPR and Sortilin [<citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201806153" pmid="30559172" pmcid="PMC6363445" count="1">105</citation>-<citation rid="CR107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2014.11.027" pmid="25533483" pmcid="PMC4289081" count="1">107</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Vps35/Vps26 interacts with Sortilin via the sorting motif YSVL and mutagenesis of this site impairs the binding with Vps35/Vps26 [<citation rid="CR108" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2007.12.015" pmid="18078806" count="1">108</citation>]. <sentence_start/>CI-MPR trafficking can be mediated by the retromer or ESCPE-1 [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41556-019-0393-3" pmid="31576058" pmcid="PMC6778059" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201702137" pmid="28935632" pmcid="PMC5674888" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX6, a component of the ESCPE-1 complex, directly interacts with RAB32 through its phox homology (PX) domain and this interaction is linked to the recycling of CI-MPR to the TGN [<citation rid="CR109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0208889" pmid="30640902" pmcid="PMC6331118" count="1">109</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ESCPE-1 recognizes two antiparallel β-strands, βA and βB, of a β-hairpin-shaped sorting motif in CI-MPR. <sentence_start/>Through this interaction, ESCPE-1 carries CI-MPR from the endosomes to the TGN [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41556-019-0393-3" pmid="31576058" pmcid="PMC6778059" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer controls CI-MPR trafficking directly via interaction between the cytosolic domain of CI-MPR and hVPS35 [<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312055" pmid="15078903" pmcid="PMC2172094" count="1">104</citation>], or indirectly via Sortilin-related receptor 1 (SORL1, also known as SORLA), a retromer cargo [<citation rid="CR110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.stemcr.2023.10.011" pmcid="PMC10724056" pmid="37949073" count="1">110</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SORLA directly binds VPS26 via a phenylalanine residue located in a six-amino acid FANSHY sequence in the SORLA tail [<citation rid="CR111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4161/cib.21433" pmid="23740096" pmcid="PMC3541330" count="1">111</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SORL1 levels were found to be decreased in AD brains [<citation rid="CR112" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-014-8742-5" pmid="24833601" count="1">112</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In SORL1-deficient human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived microglia-like cells, CI-MPR has reduced expression and reduced co-localization with enzymes in lysosomes, highlighting how CI-MPR levels and localization are intertwined with SORL1 [<citation rid="CR113" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/glia.70009" pmcid="PMC12121473" pmid="40183375" count="1">113</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Retrograde protein trafficking to the TGN: </italic>The retromer-dependent retrograde cargo trafficking requires SNX3 [<citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201806153" pmid="30559172" pmcid="PMC6363445" count="1">105</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX3 facilitates retromer’s localization to the endosomal membrane [<citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2012.04.020" pmcid="PMC3391348" pmid="22673115" count="1">93</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX3 predominantly localizes to the early endosomes and is involved in retrograde protein trafficking to the TGN [<citation rid="CR114" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb2281" pmid="21725319" pmcid="PMC4052212" count="1">114</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX3 sorting role resides in binding PI3P on early endosomes via the phox-homolog domain [<citation rid="CR11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/35083051" pmid="11433298" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Via this function, SNX3 regulates the transport of different transmembrane proteins such as CI-MPR (Fig. 5), Wnt sorting receptor Wntless, APP, transferrin receptor (TfR) and the iron transporter Fet3/Ftr1 [<citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201806153" pmid="30559172" pmcid="PMC6363445" count="1">105</citation>, <citation rid="CR114" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb2281" pmid="21725319" pmcid="PMC4052212" count="1">114</citation>-<citation rid="CR117" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2013.01.013" pmid="23416069" pmcid="PMC3595351" count="1">117</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In HEK293T cells, overexpression of SNX3 correlates with decreased APP internalization, higher levels on the plasma membrane and decreased levels of secreted Aβ, which points towards a SNX3-mediated salvage of APP from the intracellular amyloidogenic pathway [<citation rid="CR115" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000486199" pmid="29414832" pmcid="PMC5916825" count="1">115</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The evidence of SNX3 involvement in AD is further strengthened by the identification of SNX3 polymorphisms associated with the risk of AD [<citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2012.04.020" pmcid="PMC3391348" pmid="22673115" count="1">93</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Further details of how the SNX3 impacts PD are further discussed in the oxidative stress subparagraph.

<italic toggle="yes">Transmembrane protein sorting to the plasma membrane:</italic> A retromer adaptor relevant in protein sorting to the plasma membrane is SNX27. <sentence_start/>SNX27 contains an N-terminal domain with PSD95, Dlg1, and zo-1 (PDZ), which binds VPS26A and many synaptic receptors [<citation rid="CR118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1410552111" pmid="25136126" pmcid="PMC4156734" count="1">118</citation>, <citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201004060" pmid="20733053" pmcid="PMC2928020" count="1">119</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An exposed β-hairpin in the SNX27 PDZ engages a groove in the arrestin-like structure of VPS26A [<citation rid="CR118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1410552111" pmid="25136126" pmcid="PMC4156734" count="1">118</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Different synaptic receptors interact with SNX27 via the class I PDZ-binding motifs (PDZbms) (S/T-x-Φ) and form a high or low affinity bond [<citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201004060" pmid="20733053" pmcid="PMC2928020" count="1">119</citation>, <citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb.3290" pmid="27595347" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Acidic residues (Asp/Glu) located − 3 and/or − 5 positions upstream of the PDZbms are negatively charged and interact with a positively charged and conserved Arg58 on SNX27, significantly enhancing binding affinity [<citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb.3290" pmid="27595347" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>β<sub>2</sub> adrenergic receptor (β2AR) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors lack these upstream sequences and instead have a conserved phosphorylation site for Ser/Thr residues − 3, −5 or -6 positions upstream of the PDZbms that dramatically enhances interactions with SNX27 [<citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb.3290" pmid="27595347" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, SNX27 contains the 4.1/ezrin/radixin/moesin (FERM)-like domain, able to bind Ras GTPase and a DLF motif within the N-termini of SNX1/2 [<citation rid="CR121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1017110108" pmid="21512128" pmcid="PMC3093529" count="1">121</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, a FERM-like domain is also present on SNX17, a cargo adaptor of the retriever and not of the retromer complex [<citation rid="CR122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-018-0053-7" pmid="30194414" count="1">122</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The FERM domain on SNX17 has been shown to bind the Asn-Pro-Xaa-Tyr (NPxY) sequences on the APP cytoplasmic tail [<citation rid="CR121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1017110108" pmid="21512128" pmcid="PMC3093529" count="1">121</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, SNX27 does not recycle NPxY-containing cargo, highlighting how the FERM domain on different SNXs mediates distinct endocytic recycling pathways [<citation rid="CR123" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2105510118" pmcid="PMC8433557" pmid="34462354" count="1">123</citation>].

Through these direct interactions, SNX27 traffics retromer cargoes from the endosome to the plasma membrane in a handover mechanism with ESCPE-1 and indirectly segregates retromer cargo proteins in specific endosomal areas via a FAM21-mediated interaction with the WASH complex [<citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3001601" pmid="35417450" pmcid="PMC9038204" count="1">20</citation>, <citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2405041121" pmid="39116126" pmcid="PMC11331091" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201004060" pmid="20733053" pmcid="PMC2928020" count="1">119</citation>, <citation rid="CR124" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb2374" pmid="22193161" pmcid="PMC3613977" count="1">124</citation>, <citation rid="CR125" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb2721" pmid="23563491" pmcid="PMC4052425" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27 is also identified as a regulator of transmembrane protein sorting to the cell membrane via the Golgi-independent unconventional protein secretion under cellular stress [<citation rid="CR126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-026-71409-9" pmcid="PMC13230525" pmid="41942457" count="1">126</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27 modulates unconventional protein secretion along with the VPS26A-containing retromer complex [<citation rid="CR126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-026-71409-9" pmcid="PMC13230525" pmid="41942457" count="1">126</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27 deficiency has been identified in Down syndrome (DS) brains and <italic toggle="yes">Snx27</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>−/−</sup></italic> mice presented synaptic and APP processing dysfunction [<citation rid="CR127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3117" pmid="23524343" pmcid="PMC3911880" count="1">127</citation>, <citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2014.09.037" pmid="25437557" pmcid="PMC4328673" count="1">128</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27’s role in neurodegenerative mechanisms is further explored in the proteostasis and neurotransmission section of this review.

<italic toggle="yes">RAB GTPases regulation:</italic> Endosomal recycling is regulated through an endosomal nanodomain, the retrieval subdomain, physically distinct from the ESCRT-demarcated degradative subdomains [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-61802-1" pmid="40738907" pmcid="PMC12311110" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This subdomain integrates cargo recycling with the regulated switching of specific RAB GTPases [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-61802-1" pmid="40738907" pmcid="PMC12311110" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer directly associates and recruits the RAB10 regulators DENND4A, DENND4C, TBC1D1 and TBC1D4, the RAB10 effector and RAB35 GTPase-activating protein TBC1D13, and the RAB7 GTPase-activating protein TBC1D5 to regulate the function of the retrieval subdomain [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.201797128" pmid="29158324" pmcid="PMC5770787" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-61802-1" pmid="40738907" pmcid="PMC12311110" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A conserved hydrophobic cavity on VPS29 (defined by Leu152) interacts with Pro-Leu motifs on TBC1D5, DENND4A and DENND4C, whereas VPS35 interacts with an Ile-Pro-Phe motif on TBC1D5 [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-61802-1" pmid="40738907" pmcid="PMC12311110" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>TBC1D13 envelops VPS29 using an extensive clamp structure composed of two loop sequences and interacts through three notable interfaces [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-61802-1" pmid="40738907" pmcid="PMC12311110" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, the retromer has been proposed as a mediator for GTPase regulation in the retrieval subdomain [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-61802-1" pmid="40738907" pmcid="PMC12311110" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the retrieval subdomain dysfunction is associated with neurodegeneration [<citation rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tins.2017.08.003" pmid="28962801" pmcid="PMC5654621" count="1">74</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Recruitment of RAB7a through the retromer-TBC1D5 complex enables the correct sorting of autophagy-related protein 9a (ATG9a) and autophagosome formation around damaged mitochondria during Parkin-mediated mitophagy [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.201797128" pmid="29158324" pmcid="PMC5770787" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence suggests that the retromer is at the cornerstone between ELS and mitochondrial dynamics. <sentence_start/>How the retromer-mediated regulation of RAB proteins impacts specific mechanisms of neurodegeneration is discussed in the following paragraphs.
Retromer-mediated regulation of the endosomal-lysosomal system modulates key neurodegenerative mechanisms

The authors of this review postulate a novel theoretical model of neurodegeneration, in which dysfunctional retromer subunits in AD, PD and ALS are responsible for the impairment of the ELS homeostasis, which in turn, triggers downstream neurodegenerative mechanisms (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>As previously stated, in a 2025 large-scale high-throughput proteomic study led by the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium, impaired proteostasis, neurotransmission, mitochondrial homeostasis, and neuroinflammation were converging biological pathways across neurodegenerative diseases centered around the ELS (Fig. 1) [<citation rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-025-03834-0" pmcid="PMC12353841" pmid="40665048" count="1">87</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To follow is an in-depth discussion of how the retromer affects each one of these mechanisms. <sentence_start/>In particular, via the regulation of the ELS and endosomal-mediated protein trafficking, the retromer plays a role in (i) proteostasis, protein misfolding and aggregation; (ii) mitochondrial homeostasis via regulation of proteins involved in fusion, fission, mitophagy and mitochondrial-related reactive oxidative species (ROS) production; (iii) synaptic function by controlling synaptic growth, synaptic receptor recycling and neurotransmitter reuptake; (iv) neuroinflammation, by monocyte and microglia regulation (Table 1).

Protein misfolding and aggregation into toxic multimers with loss of the physiological function of the misfolded proteins have been traditional mechanisms proposed for different neurodegenerative diseases, with Aβ and hyperphosphorylated tau for AD, αS for PD, and SOD1 and TDP-43 for ALS [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrn3406" pmid="23254192" pmcid="PMC4295774" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/cshperspect.a024117" pmcid="PMC5538408" pmid="28003278" count="1">57</citation>, <citation rid="CR130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.4443" pmid="29200205" pmcid="PMC5760353" count="1">130</citation>, <citation rid="CR131" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnmol.2019.00025" pmid="30837838" pmcid="PMC6382748" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, the hypothesis that reducing the amount of these toxic aggregates would be neuroprotective has been the subject of investigations and debate for decades [<citation rid="CR132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/emm.2014.117" pmid="25766616" pmcid="PMC4351408" count="1">132</citation>].

The retromer has a key role in proteostasis via the endosomal network and the regulation of the trafficking of proteins involved in cellular catabolic pathways, i.e. ELS itself, macroautophagy (MA), chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) [<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312055" pmid="15078903" pmcid="PMC2172094" count="1">104</citation>, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms4828" pmid="24819384" pmcid="PMC4024763" count="1">133</citation>, <citation rid="CR134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0042-15.2015" pmid="26203154" pmcid="PMC4510296" count="1">134</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These pathways are intertwined via significant cross-talk, leading to a reciprocal modulation in which the retromer is involved [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>, <citation rid="CR135" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-024-00757-5" pmid="39107446" pmcid="PMC12239022" count="1">135</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ELS, MA, CMA, UPS are essential for neuronal proteostasis through the maintenance of a subset of the proteome with a higher risk of misfolding than the general proteome [<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312055" pmid="15078903" pmcid="PMC2172094" count="1">104</citation>, <citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms4828" pmid="24819384" pmcid="PMC4024763" count="1">133</citation>, <citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.03.048" pmid="33891876" pmcid="PMC8152331" count="1">136</citation>-<citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/JIR.S342096" pmid="35002279" pmcid="PMC8721160" count="1">138</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These pathways have been demonstrated to be altered in patient samples or pre-clinical models of ALS, PD and AD, with consequent accumulation of toxic misfolded proteins (Table 1) [<citation rid="CR139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/biomedicines9111625" pmcid="PMC8615936" pmid="34829854" count="1">139</citation>-<citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1098/rstb.2022.0387" pmid="38368936" pmcid="PMC10874701" count="1">141</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Macroautophagy:</italic> VPS35 governs macroautophagy by controlling the trafficking of ATG9A, the only transmembrane protein of growing autophagosomes [<citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2020.107837" pmid="32610138" pmcid="PMC7388177" count="1">142</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The adequate sorting of ATG9A is coordinated by RAB7A, whose functionality is in turn regulated by VPS35 and VPS29 [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.201797128" pmid="29158324" pmcid="PMC5770787" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, VPS35 controls the localization of the WASH complex, a multiprotein structure involved in actin polymerization and consequent endosomal tubulation and scission [<citation rid="CR143" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2021.658865" pmid="33869225" pmcid="PMC8047104" count="1">143</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The WASH complex is necessary for autophagosome formation [<citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms4828" pmid="24819384" pmcid="PMC4024763" count="1">133</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 governs MA also by controlling the WASH complex’s sorting and recycling via direct interaction with one of its subunits, the protein FAM21 (Fig. 3) [<citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2405041121" pmid="39116126" pmcid="PMC11331091" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/pro.4980" pmid="38607248" pmcid="PMC11010949" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR143" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2021.658865" pmid="33869225" pmcid="PMC8047104" count="1">143</citation>, <citation rid="CR144" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.devcel.2012.12.014" pmid="23369714" count="1">144</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">CMA:</italic> VPS35 directs CMA by sorting lysosome-associated membrane protein 2 A (LAMP2A), a protein receptor located on lysosomes (Fig. 3) [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>, <citation rid="CR134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0042-15.2015" pmid="26203154" pmcid="PMC4510296" count="1">134</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> KO cell multi-omics analysis revealed LAMP2 displacement to the cell membrane, which may be secondary to the enhanced lysosomal exocytosis identified in <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> KO cells and highlights the retromer’s role in appropriate LAMP2 positioning on the lysosomal cell membrane [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>]. <sentence_start/>CMA regulates the degradation of cytosolic proteins carrying a CMA recognition motif such as KFERQ. <sentence_start/>The KFERQ motif is recognized by the chaperone proteins heat shock protein 8/heat shock cognate protein 70 (HSPA8/HSC70), which sorts the substrate to lysosomes (Fig. 3). <sentence_start/>The substrate binds LAMP2A and the complex is internalized into the lysosomes, where LAMP2A dissociates for recycling, whereas the cytosolic protein will be degraded by lysosomal hydrolases [<citation rid="CR145" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/15548627.2019.1603545" pmid="30983487" pmcid="PMC6984454" count="1">145</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">UPS:</italic> A significant increase in poly-ubiquitinylated protein levels was identified in <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic>-downregulated brain endothelial cells or embryonic neurons, which points towards a regulatory role of the retromer in the UPS system function [<citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/JIR.S342096" pmid="35002279" pmcid="PMC8721160" count="1">138</citation>, <citation rid="CR146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-019-0487-2" pmid="31907392" pmcid="PMC7308361" count="1">146</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A direct or indirect interaction between the retromer and the proteasome has yet to be demonstrated.

<italic toggle="yes">Alzheimer's disease:</italic> There are three mechanisms related to endosomal system dysfunction through which the retromer is involved in amyloid and tau pathology in AD: (i) production of toxic forms of amyloid and tau, (ii) their reduced clearance and (iii) dysfunctional recycling of APP [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>, <citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110182" pmid="34965419" pmcid="PMC8792909" count="1">94</citation>, <citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0802545105" pmid="18480253" pmcid="PMC2386077" count="1">96</citation>, <citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/JIR.S342096" pmid="35002279" pmcid="PMC8721160" count="1">138</citation>, <citation rid="CR147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110262" pmid="35045281" pmcid="PMC8830374" count="1">147</citation>, <citation rid="CR148" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mcn.2018.09.003" pmid="30257187" count="1">148</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Impaired production:</italic> The retromer cargo adaptor SNX27 regulates γ-secretase activity via interaction with the presenilin-1 subunit of this complex in vitro and in vivo [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2014.09.037" pmid="25437557" pmcid="PMC4328673" count="1">128</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reduced SNX27 expression leads to markedly increased Aβ generation and reduced APP levels [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2014.09.037" pmid="25437557" pmcid="PMC4328673" count="1">128</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27 overexpression decreases Aβ generation in the hippocampus of Tg2576 mice harboring the Swedish familial mutation in human <italic toggle="yes">AAP</italic> mice [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2014.09.037" pmid="25437557" pmcid="PMC4328673" count="1">128</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence highlights SNX27’s role in regulating Aβ generation by modulating γ-secretase activity [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2014.09.037" pmid="25437557" pmcid="PMC4328673" count="1">128</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Reduced clearance:</italic> Sortilin and CI-MPR are two retromer cargoes involved in carrying lysosomal hydrolases to the lysosomes (Fig. 5) [<citation rid="CR149" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/emboj/20.9.2180" pmid="11331584" pmcid="PMC125444" count="1">149</citation>, <citation rid="CR150" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312034" pmid="15078902" pmcid="PMC2172078" count="1">150</citation>]. <sentence_start/>CI-MPR is deficient in the AD model of hiPSC-derived microglia-like cells, and decreased expression levels of Sortilin, CI-MPR, cathepsin D (CTSD), VPS35, VPS26, and VPS29 have been detected in the cortex of Tg2576 mice expressing human APP with the Swedish mutation (K670N/M671L) [<citation rid="CR151" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2016.12.025" pmid="28110103" count="1">151</citation>, <citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-019-0350-4" pmid="31964406" pmcid="PMC6975032" count="1">152</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In AD mouse models, the axonal retrograde transport of VPS35 and VPS26 is impaired, and retromer-mediated CI-MPR retrieval is disrupted, causing protease deficiency in lysosomes and impaired lysosomal proteolysis [<citation rid="CR153" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddx321" pmid="28973312" pmcid="PMC5886073" count="1">153</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similar findings have yet to be demonstrated for Sortilin in AD preclinical models. <sentence_start/>The retromer enhancer R55 diminishes Aβ peptide levels, pointing towards a retromer-mediated reduction of APP processing and overall retromer function in limiting the generation of toxic amyloid [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer enhancer R33 led to an increase in VPS35, VPS26, and VPS29, CI-MPR, and CTSD levels and to a reduction in beta-amyloid levels, accompanied by improved memory and synaptic integrity [<citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-019-0350-4" pmid="31964406" pmcid="PMC6975032" count="1">152</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These data suggest the retromer’s role in modulating the clearance of Aβ and tau via the distribution of the lysosomal hydrolases-carrying protein CI-MPR, and lysosomal hydrolases within the ELS system (Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>In vivo and in vitro ALS and PD models manipulated with retromer enhancers registered an increase in levels of the mature form of CTSD [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>, <citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Further studies are needed to investigate the relationship between the retromer and mature forms of cathepsins in AD.

In AD mouse models, CMA plays a key role in maintaining neuronal proteostasis of the proteome subset with a higher risk of misfolding [<citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.03.048" pmid="33891876" pmcid="PMC8152331" count="1">136</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Tau and APP are potential targets for CMA-mediated clearance [<citation rid="CR156" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-018-0001-6" pmid="29626215" pmcid="PMC6399518" count="1">156</citation>, <citation rid="CR157" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5483/BMBRep.2016.49.6.212" pmid="26779997" pmcid="PMC5070722" count="1">157</citation>]. <sentence_start/>At their C-terminus, tau has multiple KFERQ-like motifs, and APP contains one KFERQ motif [<citation rid="CR156" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-018-0001-6" pmid="29626215" pmcid="PMC6399518" count="1">156</citation>, <citation rid="CR157" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5483/BMBRep.2016.49.6.212" pmid="26779997" pmcid="PMC5070722" count="1">157</citation>]. <sentence_start/>HSC70, a key mediator of CMA, binds the KFERQ recognition motif [<citation rid="CR156" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-018-0001-6" pmid="29626215" pmcid="PMC6399518" count="1">156</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Early evidence in PD revealed that VPS35 enhancement is associated with increased HSC70 levels [<citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>, <citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000204465" count="1">158</citation>], though this has yet to be demonstrated in AD models.

<italic toggle="yes">Dysfunctional recycling:</italic> SORL1 is involved in the sorting of APP from the endosomes to the TGN and plasma membrane, preventing amyloidogenic processing (Fig. 2) [<citation rid="CR159" ref-type="bibr" count="1">159</citation>, <citation rid="CR160" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4103/1673-5374.170288" pmid="26807092" pmcid="PMC4705769" count="1">160</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In SORL1-deficient hiPSC-derived microglia-like cells, amyloid beta 1-42 accumulates [<citation rid="CR113" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/glia.70009" pmcid="PMC12121473" pmid="40183375" count="1">113</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SORL1 exerts its sorting effect via interaction with Vps26b [<citation rid="CR159" ref-type="bibr" count="1">159</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Silencing <italic toggle="yes">Vps26b</italic> in mice significantly decreases SORL1 levels in the plasma membrane and increases Aβ and tau accumulation in brain tissue and CSF [<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110182" pmid="34965419" pmcid="PMC8792909" count="1">94</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These data suggest how impaired APP recycling secondary to the ELS dysfunction can be a pathogenetic mechanism of AD.

<italic toggle="yes">Parkinson’s disease:</italic> Emerging data have highlighted the MA, ELS, and CMA contributions to αS degradation (Fig. 3) [<citation rid="CR161" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18172548" doi="10.1172/JCI32806" pmcid="PMC2157565" count="1">161</citation>-<citation rid="CR164" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1500937112" pmid="26170293" pmcid="PMC4522768" count="1">164</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In transgenic mice overexpressing human αS, the lentiviral-delivered expression of human VPS35 rescues αS-induced neurodegeneration [<citation rid="CR107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2014.11.027" pmid="25533483" pmcid="PMC4289081" count="1">107</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, retromer enhancement with the molecular chaperone 1,3 bis-phenyl guanylhydrazone (or 2a) protects against neurodegeneration and favors αS clearance in a PD mouse model, potentially due to the upregulation of the αS degradation pathways, CMA, ELS, and MA [<citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>, <citation rid="CR165" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.csbj.2024.02.026" pmid="38487369" pmcid="PMC10937258" count="1">165</citation>, <citation rid="CR166" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000208527" count="1">166</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In in vivo and in vitro models of PD, 2a increases the levels of LAMP2A, HSC70, markers of MA, and favors the endosome-to-Golgi retrieval of LAMP2A, increases light chain 3-II (LC3-II) and decreases p62 (an αS receptor), indicating enhanced MA flux [<citation rid="CR167" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41419-017-0121-5" pmid="29367588" pmcid="PMC5833699" count="1">167</citation>, <citation rid="CR168" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1508-21.2022" pmid="35169022" pmcid="PMC8985870" count="1">168</citation>], increases levels of the mature forms of CTSD, modulates cathepsin L (CTSL) levels and lysosomal hydrolases carriers Sortilin and CI-MPR, indicating an
