enhanced lysosomal activity, with subsequent reduction in pathological αS levels [<citation rid="CR134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0042-15.2015" pmid="26203154" pmcid="PMC4510296" count="1">134</citation>, <citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>, <citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000204465" count="1">158</citation>, <citation rid="CR166" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000208527" count="1">166</citation>, <citation rid="CR169" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/gtc.13099" pmid="38366711" count="1">169</citation>, <citation rid="CR170" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adj1205" pmid="38091401" pmcid="PMC10848721" count="1">170</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Pharmacological inhibition of LRRK2 in <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> cells did not affect CTSL levels [<citation rid="CR170" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adj1205" pmid="38091401" pmcid="PMC10848721" count="1">170</citation>], highlighting the retromer-dependent modulation of CTSL levels. <sentence_start/>Of note, αS carries the KFERQ recognition motif recognized by the chaperone proteins HSPA8/HSC70, which sorts the substrate to LAMP2A, favoring αS degradation via CMA (Fig. 3) [<citation rid="CR171" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3000301" pmid="31150375" pmcid="PMC6561683" count="1">171</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Retromer binding to FAM21 and the WASH complex is perturbed by the PD-linked <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic><sup>D620N</sup> mutation, with VPS3<italic toggle="yes">5</italic><sup>D620N</sup> forming clusters with FAM21 in EEs and disrupting MA (Fig. 3) [<citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms4828" pmid="24819384" pmcid="PMC4024763" count="1">133</citation>, <citation rid="CR172" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2014.06.024" pmid="24980502" pmcid="PMC4110399" count="1">172</citation>, <citation rid="CR173" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13041-021-00848-w" pmid="34530877" pmcid="PMC8447518" count="1">173</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer governs ELS also by its interaction with RAB proteins and LRRK2, whose mutations have been associated with familial PD [<citation rid="CR174" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ana.10113" pmid="11891824" count="1">174</citation>-<citation rid="CR176" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2004.11.005" pmid="15541309" count="1">176</citation>]. <sentence_start/>LRRK2 inhibits the lysosomal degradative activity, as well as regulates proper vesicular transport and autophagy via interaction with RAB GTPases, among which RAB10 [<citation rid="CR177" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awx344" pmid="29253086" pmcid="PMC5837795" count="1">177</citation>-<citation rid="CR179" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-018-0240-1" pmcid="PMC5811984" pmid="29439717" count="1">179</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35<sup>D620N</sup> recruits and activates LRRK2 on the lysosomal surface, driving assembly of the RILPL1-TMEM55B complex, which coordinates autophagosome formation and lysosomal repair [<citation rid="CR170" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adj1205" pmid="38091401" pmcid="PMC10848721" count="1">170</citation>, <citation rid="CR180" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-44316-6" pmid="38168055" pmcid="PMC10761734" count="1">180</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 can protect against neuronal death caused by LRRK2 mutations, suggesting that VPS35 overexpression may mitigate some of the toxic effects associated with LRRK2 hyperactivity via a functional interaction [<citation rid="CR181" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1750-1326-9-23" pmid="24915984" pmcid="PMC4126812" count="1">181</citation>] and rescue the neurodegenerative phenotype induced by LRRK2 [<citation rid="CR177" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awx344" pmid="29253086" pmcid="PMC5837795" count="1">177</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 modulates the levels of RAB27b [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>], a modulator of lysosomal exocytosis and cell-to-cell transmission of pathogenic αS aggregates [<citation rid="CR182" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.RA120.013337" pmid="32350025" pmcid="PMC7278354" count="1">182</citation>, <citation rid="CR183" ref-type="bibr" count="1">183</citation>] and of RAB39b, a regulator of αS accumulation [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>, <citation rid="CR184" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2014.10.015" pmid="25434005" pmcid="PMC4259921" count="1">184</citation>, <citation rid="CR185" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pgen.1005995" pmid="27123591" pmcid="PMC4849646" count="1">185</citation>].

However, Chen et al. found that VPS35 depletion fails to increase levels of endogenous αS protein in SH-SY5Y cells and that genetic overexpression of wild-type VPS35 in Sprague-Dawley rats does not prevent αS accumulation, nor protect against αS-induced nigral dopaminergic neurodegeneration [<citation rid="CR186" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-023-00641-4" pmid="37542299" pmcid="PMC10403858" count="1">186</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence contrasts with the prior body of evidence highlighting that <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> loss of function enhances αS accumulation within the lysosomes, and αS toxicity in yeast, worms, and mouse and emerging evidence highlighting 2a-mediated enhancement of VPS35 function protects against neurodegeneration and favors αS clearance [<citation rid="CR107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2014.11.027" pmid="25533483" pmcid="PMC4289081" count="1">107</citation>, <citation rid="CR187" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2014.07.014" pmid="25107340" count="1">187</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Differences in these results may reflect different retromer manipulation methods, i.e. genetic overexpression versus pharmacological modulation. <sentence_start/>While genetic approaches may induce sustained and potentially supraphysiological increases in protein expression, pharmacological modulation may achieve a more controlled enhancement of retromer activity, potentially leading to different retromer functional outcomes and cellular responses. <sentence_start/>Second, retromer structure depends on the coordinated assembly of multiple subunits [<citation rid="CR188" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0854.2010.01124.x" pmid="20875039" count="1">188</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Disproportionate changes in concentration of individual subunits could disrupt complex stability, leading to aberrant protein interactions and impaired retromer functionality [<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312055" pmid="15078903" pmcid="PMC2172094" count="1">104</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this context, it is relevant that 2a increases the levels of all the subunits of the retromer, VPS35, VPS26b and VPS29 subunits, whereas in Chen et al. investigation, selective genetic overexpression of VPS35 was implemented [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>, <citation rid="CR186" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-023-00641-4" pmid="37542299" pmcid="PMC10403858" count="1">186</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Thus, while moderate and balanced enhancement of retromer component expression may promote retromer activity, excessive and/or unbalanced overexpression may paradoxically compromise retromer function. <sentence_start/>To address these questions, it will be essential to evaluate whether genetic overexpression effectively enhances retromer function by assessing the trafficking, localization, and protein levels of established retromer cargoes and lysosomal hydrolases, including CI-MPR, LAMP2A, and CTSD. <sentence_start/>These analyses will help determine whether the intervention improves endosomal-lysosomal trafficking and cargo recycling in a functionally meaningful manner.

<italic toggle="yes">Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis:</italic> Similarly, in ALS mouse models, the retromer enhancer 2a increases the levels of mature CTSD and CI-MPR, reduces the levels of misfolded SOD1, and rescues motor neurons in a SOD1 mouse model, highlighting that the retromer protects against neurodegeneration by boosting SOD degradation via the ELS [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In ALS MNs, declining expression of retromer components (VPS26A, VPS26B, VPS29, VPS35), SNX6 and SNX12 accompanies increasing presence of TDP-43 + cytoplasmic inclusions, which supports the hypothesis that retromer complex-mediated endolysosomal sorting is involved in the formation or clearance of TDP-43 inclusions (Fig. 4) [<citation rid="CR101" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2023.113636" pmid="38183652" pmcid="PMC10926001" count="1">101</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Impaired TDP-43 clearance leads to its mislocalization within neurons and subsequent alternative polyadenylation of the 3’ untranslated region of the <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> transcript [<citation rid="CR189" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3003573" pmid="41490046" pmcid="PMC12768243" count="1">189</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This is associated with reduced VPS35 and VPS29 protein expression, which in turn leads to ELS dysfunction, TDP-43 accumulation and hyperphosphorylation [<citation rid="CR189" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3003573" pmid="41490046" pmcid="PMC12768243" count="1">189</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This mechanism has been demonstrated in patients with frontotemporal dementia [<citation rid="CR189" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.3003573" pmid="41490046" pmcid="PMC12768243" count="1">189</citation>], a neurodegenerative disorder with significant genetic and clinical overlap with ALS [<citation rid="CR190" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnins.2020.00042" pmid="32116499" pmcid="PMC7012787" count="1">190</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The impairment of an upstream retromer and endosomal trafficking regulator, NIMA-related kinase 1 (NEK1), whose mutation is associated with ~ 3% of ALS cases, reiterates the key role the retromer plays in modulating the ELS in the context of ALS pathophysiology (Fig. 4) [<citation rid="CR191" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3626" pmid="27455347" pmcid="PMC5560030" count="1">191</citation>].

Overall, this retromer function is of potential relevance to the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, characterized by the accumulation of misfolded, toxic proteins. <sentence_start/>Pharmacological enhancement or genetic overexpression of the retromer cargo-binding subunit VPS35 has been shown to boost these misfolded protein degradation pathways, decreasing the levels of misfolded proteins and favoring the rescue of the neurodegenerative processes [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>, <citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-019-0350-4" pmid="31964406" pmcid="PMC6975032" count="1">152</citation>, <citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>, <citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000204465" count="1">158</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, retromer enhancement may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for the clearance of toxic aggregates typical of these neurodegenerative diseases and a common approach based on overlapping pathogenetic mechanisms. <sentence_start/>The effect of retromer enhancement to increase the levels of cellular chaperones such as HSC70, which also have a role in reverting the misfolded state [<citation rid="CR192" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0968-0004(02)02125-4" pmid="12114026" count="1">192</citation>], may represent an additional strategy through which retromer enhancement can impact neurodegeneration, though this still needs to be investigated.
Mitochondrial homeostasis, biogenesis, and oxidative stress

Mitochondrial homeostasis, the equilibrium between mitochondrial fusion and fission, and the oxidative reaction chain can be disrupted in PD, AD, and ALS [<citation rid="CR193" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-023-04493-w" pmcid="PMC10493034" pmid="37689642" count="1">193</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer modulates mitochondrial fusion, fission, mitophagy, mitochondrial-related ROS production, dampens ROS-mediated damage and prevents apoptosis (Table 1) [<citation rid="CR194" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2020.105056" pmid="32853677" count="1">194</citation>-<citation rid="CR197" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adr6415" pmid="40184468" pmcid="PMC11970507" count="1">197</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Overall, the preclinical data on the retromer’s involvement in mitochondrial functionality in AD mainly relate to its role in modulating oxidative stress and oxidative stress-related damage by favoring glial lipid droplets (LD) formation, a sequestration site for peroxidized lipids (Fig. 6) [<citation rid="CR198" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2112095118" pmcid="PMC8719885" pmid="34949639" count="1">198</citation>, <citation rid="CR199" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.202102136" pmcid="PMC8222944" pmid="34152362" count="1">199</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Despite evidence of altered mitochondrial activity in ALS, further studies are necessary to investigate whether retromer-mediated modulation plays a role in this feature.

Retromer role in neurotransmission and oxidative stress in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Neurotransmission: (i) Decrease in AMPA receptor (AMPAR) levels and increased AMPA ubiquitination, with consequent neuronal internalization and proteasomal degradation; (ii) Retromer loss leads to increased release of cargoes, such as Amyloid Precursor Proteins (APP), in Neuronal Extracellular Vesicles (NEVs) due to cargo accumulation at the motor neuron presynaptic terminals. <sentence_start/>NEVs are released by neurons; (iii) The retromer is responsible for the trafficking and surface recycling of Glutamate Receptor Subunit A1 (GluA1). <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Oxidative stress: retromer favors glial lipid droplets formation, a sequestration site for peroxidized lipids, which are a typical mediator of ROS-induced cell injury. <sentence_start/>Created in

<italic toggle="yes">Parkinson’s disease:</italic> Dopaminergic neurons of idiopathic PD patients demonstrate an impaired ability to turn over mitochondria and maintain mitochondrial proteostasis due to alterations in mitochondrial quality control proteins, such as parkin, PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1), and mitofusin 2 (MNF2) [<citation rid="CR200" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41531-023-00564-3" pmid="37553379" pmcid="PMC10409763" count="1">200</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This may exacerbate the impact of oxidative phosphorylation defects and oxidative stress, contributing to neuronal degeneration [<citation rid="CR200" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41531-023-00564-3" pmid="37553379" pmcid="PMC10409763" count="1">200</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer is a critical player in mitochondrial quality control protein pathways.

<italic toggle="yes">Fusion and fission:</italic> VPS35 gene deletion in dopamine (DA) neurons results in mitochondrial fragmentation, highlighting altered processes of fusion and fission [<citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2015.08.001" pmid="26321632" pmcid="PMC4565770" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>MFN2 and DRP1 are involved in fusion and fission, respectively.

Mitochondrial fusion involves the activity of two main proteins, MFN1 and MFN2 and optic atrophy 1 (OPA1) proteins [<citation rid="CR201" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/brv.12378" pmid="29068134" pmcid="PMC6446723" count="1">201</citation>]. <sentence_start/>MFN2 is ubiquitinated for proteasomal degradation by the mitochondrial E3-ubiquitin ligase-1 (MUL1). <sentence_start/>By promoting the degradation of MUL1, the VPS35 promotes mitochondrial fusion [<citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2015.08.001" pmid="26321632" pmcid="PMC4565770" count="1">137</citation>] (Fig. 7). <sentence_start/>VPS35 deficiency increased MUL1, leading to MFN2 degradation in DA neurons (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2015.08.001" pmid="26321632" pmcid="PMC4565770" count="1">137</citation>].

Retromer role in mitochondrial homeostasis and function in Parkinson’s disease substantia nigra. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Oxidative stress: Ferrous (Fe<sup>2+</sup>) iron attracts one electron from hydrogen peroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>), with consequent H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> monovalent reduction and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). <sentence_start/>Fe<sup>2+</sup> can be internalized by transferrin receptors, limiting its conversion into ROS. <sentence_start/>α-Synuclein inhibits transferrin receptor recycling to and from the plasma membrane, whereas the retromer facilitates this recycling. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Micromitophagy: Parkin phosphorylation by PINK1 increases parkin E3 ligase activity, leading to ubiquitination by parkin of Vps35 and formation of MDVs, which carry damaged and oxidized cargo peroxysomes. <sentence_start/>VPS35 is recruited to budding MDVs, which are rich in MAPL (also known as MUL1) and modulates MAPL trafficking to peroxisomes. <sentence_start/>(<bold>C</bold>) VPS35<sup>D620N</sup> leads to increased release of cytosolic cytochrome c and decreased interaction with PINK1. <sentence_start/>(<bold>D</bold>) Oxidative stress: Loss of PLA2 stabilizes the retromer and impairs the retrieval of ceramide phosphoethanolamine and sphingomyelin from the mitochondrial membrane to the trans-Golgi network. <sentence_start/>This leads to an increase in inner mitochondrial membrane ceramides. <sentence_start/>Ceramides interact with complex III of the electron transport chain, leading to the generation of ROS. <sentence_start/>(<bold>E</bold>) Mitochondrial fission: Dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1) assembles into a ring structure on the mitochondrial outer membrane, inducing mitochondrial fission. <sentence_start/>VPS35 binds DRP1 and assists in DRP1 recycling. <sentence_start/>The D620N <italic toggle="yes">VPS35</italic> mutation reduced DRP1-VPS35 interaction. <sentence_start/>(<bold>F</bold>) Mitochondrial fusion: Mitofusin 2 (MFN2) is ubiquitinated for proteasomal degradation by MUL1, promoting mitochondrial fusion. <sentence_start/>VPS35 deficiency increased Mitochondrial E3 Ubiquitin Protein Ligase (MUL1), leading to MFN2 degradation. <sentence_start/>Created in

Mitochondrial fission requires DRP1, also known as dynamin-like protein 1 (DLP1). <sentence_start/>DRP1 recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) assembles into a ring structure, which induces fission of mitochondria (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR202" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1091/mbc.12.8.2245" pmid="11514614" pmcid="PMC58592" count="1">202</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the carboxyl region of DRP1 contains a short phenylalanine-leucine-valine (FLV) amino acid sequence required for VPS35 binding, which has similarities to known retromer sorting motifs [<citation rid="CR203" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28040727" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddw430" pmcid="PMC5903416" count="1">203</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The VPS35 regulates mitochondrial fission by carrying DRP1 to the lysosome for degradation via an MDV-dependent route (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR203" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28040727" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddw430" pmcid="PMC5903416" count="1">203</citation>, <citation rid="CR204" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3983" pmid="26618722" pmcid="PMC4826611" count="1">204</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The D620N VPS35 mutation reduced DLP1-VPS35 interaction and increased mitochondrial fragmentation (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR203" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28040727" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddw430" pmcid="PMC5903416" count="1">203</citation>, <citation rid="CR204" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3983" pmid="26618722" pmcid="PMC4826611" count="1">204</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Mitophagy:</italic> Mitophagy is a specialized form of autophagy that regulates the turnover of damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria. <sentence_start/>Mitophagy uses ubiquitin-dependent (e.g., the PINK1-PRKN pathway) and -independent (e.g., BNIP3L/NIX, FUNDC1, and BNIP3) pathways that converge on the final common autophagic pathway. <sentence_start/>The PARK2 and PINK1 genes, whose mutations are associated with autosomal recessive juvenile PD [<citation rid="CR205" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/33416" pmid="9560156" count="1">205</citation>-<citation rid="CR207" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1096284" pmid="15087508" count="1">207</citation>], encode parkin, an E3-ubiquitin ligase [<citation rid="CR208" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/77060" pmid="10888878" count="1">208</citation>, <citation rid="CR209" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.240347797" pmid="11078524" pmcid="PMC27228" count="1">209</citation>], and the kinase PINK1. <sentence_start/>Parkin and PINK1 are involved in a ubiquitin-dependent mitophagy pathway. <sentence_start/>Upon mitochondrial damage, PINK1 accumulates on the MOM, phosphorylates adjacent ubiquitin on MOM proteins, acting as a receptor for parkin [<citation rid="CR210" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-024-58285-3" pmid="38565869" pmcid="PMC10987619" count="1">210</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Once recruited, parkin phosphorylation by PINK1 increases parkin E3 ligase activity, leading to ubiquitination by parkin of proteins on the MOM and initiation of mitophagy through engulfment in isolation membranes that then fuse with lysosomes [<citation rid="CR211" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrm3028" pmid="21179058" pmcid="PMC4780047" count="1">211</citation>].

Micromitophagy is a selective form of mitophagy of just a mitochondrial fragment, is activated by the PINK1-PRKN pathway and involves MDVs, which carry damaged and oxidized mitochondrial cargo to lysosomes and peroxysomes (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2010.05.066" pmid="20619655" count="1">67</citation>, <citation rid="CR210" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-024-58285-3" pmid="38565869" pmcid="PMC10987619" count="1">210</citation>, <citation rid="CR212" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.201488104" pmid="25107473" pmcid="PMC4282503" count="1">212</citation>, <citation rid="CR213" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.redox.2014.06.004" pmid="25009776" pmcid="PMC4085350" count="1">213</citation>]. <sentence_start/>MDVs formation is independent of the classic protein involved in mitochondrial fission and mitophagy, DRP1 [<citation rid="CR214" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.freeradbiomed.2019.12.005" pmid="31825802" count="1">214</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Budding MDVs are rich in mitochondria-associated protein ligase (MAPL, also known as MUL1), a SUMO E3-ligase whose RING finger regulates mitochondrial morphology by inducing mitochondrial fragmentation if MAPL is overexpressed [<citation rid="CR215" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcb.30114" pmid="34322908" count="1">215</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Live-cell microscopic analysis revealed that VPS35 is recruited to MDVs and VPS26A and VPS35 modulate MAPL trafficking to peroxisomes (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2010.05.066" pmid="20619655" count="1">67</citation>, <citation rid="CR215" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcb.30114" pmid="34322908" count="1">215</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The mechanisms by which the retromer is recruited to the MDVs and how its function is modulated to allow a directional transfer of MAPL are unclear. <sentence_start/>VPS35 works downstream of parkin, and parkin mediates the polyubiquitination of VPS35, which is suspected to serve as a regulatory mechanism for retromer-dependent sorting (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR216" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddy224" pmid="29893854" pmcid="PMC6121197" count="1">216</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence suggests that parkin could regulate retromer-mediated MDVs trafficking in mitophagy. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> models, <italic toggle="yes">vps35</italic> interacts genetically with <italic toggle="yes">parkin</italic>, but not <italic toggle="yes">pink1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">vps35</italic> overexpression rescues parkin-mutant phenotypes [<citation rid="CR217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddv322" pmid="26251041" pmcid="PMC4599670" count="1">217</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A loss-of-function mechanism involving parkin and mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to how the <italic toggle="yes">vps35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> mutation leads to a PD phenotype [<citation rid="CR217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddv322" pmid="26251041" pmcid="PMC4599670" count="1">217</citation>].

A novel function for MAPL in peroxisomes is the regulation of peroxisome elongation and morphology [<citation rid="CR215" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcb.30114" pmid="34322908" count="1">215</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, further studies are required to unravel if the crosstalk between the retromer and mitochondria via MAPL could signify an indirect effect of the retromer on peroxisome function.

<italic toggle="yes">Oxidative stress:</italic> Mitochondria-mediated ROS production is related to electron transport chain activity during oxidative phosphorylation [<citation rid="CR218" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-023-02907-z" pmid="38081963" count="1">218</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A leading model describes excessive ROS as the unfortunate byproduct of dysfunctional mitochondria in neurodegenerative diseases [<citation rid="CR218" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-023-02907-z" pmid="38081963" count="1">218</citation>, <citation rid="CR219" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/428010" pmid="22685618" pmcid="PMC3362933" count="1">219</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ROS induce cellular damage by modifying the structure of proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acid, including mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) [<citation rid="CR197" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adr6415" pmid="40184468" pmcid="PMC11970507" count="1">197</citation>, <citation rid="CR220" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s42255-022-00591-z" pmid="35760871" pmcid="PMC9711940" count="1">220</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Vps35</italic> expression restores mtDNA homoplasmy and alleviates associated defects in a <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> model carrying a long deletion of mtDNA [<citation rid="CR197" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adr6415" pmid="40184468" pmcid="PMC11970507" count="1">197</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Other than mitigating ROS-mediated cellular damage, the retromer also modulates mitochondrial-mediated ROS production [<citation rid="CR196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y" pmid="40140582" pmcid="PMC13005050" count="1">196</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 underlies a ROS-sensing pathway that lowers mitochondrial translation to decrease ROS levels [<citation rid="CR196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y" pmid="40140582" pmcid="PMC13005050" count="1">196</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One of these pathways includes the transporter solute carrier family 7 member 1 (SLC7A1) [<citation rid="CR196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y" pmid="40140582" pmcid="PMC13005050" count="1">196</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SLC7A1 is an Arg/Lys amino acid transporter localized on the plasma membrane and responsible for the availability of the amino acid arginine, which influences mitochondrial-tRNA (mt-tRNA) charging and consequently, mitochondrial translation [<citation rid="CR196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y" pmid="40140582" pmcid="PMC13005050" count="1">196</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Twenty-two species of mt-tRNAs encoded in mtDNA translate essential subunits of the respiratory chain complexes, which in turn are responsible for ROS production [<citation rid="CR218" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-023-02907-z" pmid="38081963" count="1">218</citation>, <citation rid="CR221" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-18068-6" pmid="32859890" pmcid="PMC7455718" count="1">221</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SLC7A1 localization and function are regulated by VPS35 [<citation rid="CR196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y" pmid="40140582" pmcid="PMC13005050" count="1">196</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Intracellular H2O2 oxidizes cysteine residues in VPS35, blocking plasma membrane localization of SLC7A1, decreasing mitochondrial translation and cellular ROS levels [<citation rid="CR196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y" pmid="40140582" pmcid="PMC13005050" count="1">196</citation>].

Stem cell-derived neurons from fibroblasts of an affected p.D620N carrier present decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and respiration, and increased production of ROS and cytosolic cytochrome c (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR222" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.28365" pmid="33142012" pmcid="PMC8048506" count="1">222</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similar evidence has been identified in mouse models, with increased levels of mitochondrial ROS, oxidative stress, and apoptotic markers found in the SN of 16-month-old Vps35<sup>D620</sup> KI mice [<citation rid="CR223" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41419-020-03228-9" pmid="33257649" pmcid="PMC7705022" count="1">223</citation>]. <sentence_start/>MPTP (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine), a prodrug of the neurotoxin MPP<sup>+,</sup> which induces PD-like pathology by causing cell death in the SN dopaminergic neurons, leads to cell injury via mitochondrial complex I inhibition and subsequent oxidative stress [<citation rid="CR224" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/syn.890180105" pmid="7825121" count="1">224</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Increased VPS35 expression protects dopaminergic neurons against MPP+ cytotoxicity. <sentence_start/>This neuroprotection function is partially inhibited by the presence of the PD-associated <italic toggle="yes">Vps35</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>D620N</sup></italic> mutation [<citation rid="CR225" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7150/ijbs.5617" pmid="23411763" pmcid="PMC3572397" count="1">225</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Together, this evidence suggests a role for the non-mutated retromer in protecting against ROS and oxidative stress.

Iron (Fe) overload can lead to oxidative stress (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR226" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbamcr.2019.118535" pmid="31446062" count="1">226</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Iron levels are increased in the SN of postmortem PD brain [<citation rid="CR227" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep36669" pmid="27827408" pmcid="PMC5101491" count="1">227</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A decrease in iron uptake due to dysfunctional transferrin receptor (TfR) could explain its accumulation in the SN of PD patients and mice [<citation rid="CR228" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-020-00698-4" pmid="33323945" pmcid="PMC8166951" count="1">228</citation>] (Fig. 7). <sentence_start/>SNX3 and VPS35 interact with the TfR to sort it to recycling endosomes (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR117" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2013.01.013" pmid="23416069" pmcid="PMC3595351" count="1">117</citation>]. <sentence_start/>αS accumulation inhibits SNX3-mediated recycling of iron transporters in <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces cerevisiae</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Caenorhabditis elegans</italic> (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddy059" pmid="29452354" count="1">116</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This evidence suggests that αS plays a role as a trigger for altered retromer function related to iron metabolism in PD patients, leading to consequent oxidative stress, neuronal injury, and neuronal death.

Under physiological conditions, mitochondria can repair ROS damage to mitochondrial membrane lipids in part via a deacylation-acylation cycle mediated by phospholipase A2 (PLA2) [<citation rid="CR229" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M604330200" pmid="16728389" pmcid="PMC1829309" count="1">229</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Loss of PLA2 disrupts retromer function, destabilizing VPS35 and VPS26 and impairing retrieval of ceramide phosphoethanolamine and sphingomyelin (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR230" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2018.05.019" pmid="29909971" count="1">230</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This leads to an increase in membrane ceramides (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR230" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2018.05.019" pmid="29909971" count="1">230</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Ceramides interact with complex III of the electron transport chain, leading to the generation of ROS, and inducing cellular oxidative stress that causes slow, progressive neurodegeneration (Fig. 7) [<citation rid="CR230" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2018.05.019" pmid="29909971" count="1">230</citation>, <citation rid="CR231" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.272.17.11369" pmid="9111045" count="1">231</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Apoptosis:</italic> The retromer enables cell survival by preventing apoptosis. <sentence_start/>Apoptosis can be triggered by two main pathways, the intrinsic and the extrinsic pathways, and mitochondria are the main actors of the intrinsic pathway [<citation rid="CR232" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13277-016-5035-9" pmid="27059734" count="1">232</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Following MOM permeabilization, cytochrome <italic toggle="yes">c</italic> is released into the cytosol, where it engages the formation of the apoptosome that leads to activation of the caspase cascade [<citation rid="CR233" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers12102853" pmcid="PMC7599739" pmid="33023187" count="1">233</citation>]. <sentence_start/>By facilitating the transport of BCL-XL, an important antiapoptotic protein, to the MOM, the VPS35 avoids MOM permeabilization and potentially avoids the release of cytochrome <italic toggle="yes">c</italic> within the cytosol [<citation rid="CR234" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1091/mbc.E19-01-0044" pmid="30840537" pmcid="PMC6724524" count="1">234</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This may account for why cells with VPS35 knockdown are more prone to apoptosis [<citation rid="CR234" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1091/mbc.E19-01-0044" pmid="30840537" pmcid="PMC6724524" count="1">234</citation>].

Neurotransmission impairment may play an important role in the pathogenesis of ALS, PD, and AD. <sentence_start/>Dopaminergic transmission is affected in PD [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrn3406" pmid="23254192" pmcid="PMC4295774" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Glutamatergic excitotoxicity and degeneration of cholinergic neurons are pathological processes of both AD and ALS [<citation rid="CR235" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/s1092852900014164" pmid="16273023" count="1">235</citation>-<citation rid="CR237" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF03160574" pmid="9178165" count="1">237</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer is present at both the neuromuscular junction pre- and post-synapse and regulates: (i) synaptic terminal growth, (ii) neurotransmitter receptor recycling, (iii) neurotransmitter reuptake in the synaptic cleft (Table 1) [<citation rid="CR146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-019-0487-2" pmid="31907392" pmcid="PMC7308361" count="1">146</citation>, <citation rid="CR217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddv322" pmid="26251041" pmcid="PMC4599670" count="1">217</citation>, <citation rid="CR238" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13041-015-0156-4" pmid="26521016" pmcid="PMC4628247" count="1">238</citation>-<citation rid="CR241" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.202012034" pmcid="PMC8144913" pmid="34019080" count="1">241</citation>].

VPS35 loss causes synaptic terminal overgrowth, increased satellite bouton number and branching formation [<citation rid="CR217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddv322" pmid="26251041" pmcid="PMC4599670" count="1">217</citation>, <citation rid="CR239" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jgg.2022.11.009" pmid="36473687" count="1">239</citation>-<citation rid="CR242" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddx179" pmid="28482024" count="1">242</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The VPS35 limits synaptic growth by coordinating with TBC1D5 to regulate RAB7 activity [<citation rid="CR239" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jgg.2022.11.009" pmid="36473687" count="1">239</citation>]. <sentence_start/>TBC1D5 is recruited to the retromer through binding to VPS29 [<citation rid="CR243" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms13305" pmid="27827364" pmcid="PMC5105194" count="1">243</citation>], a process that is impaired in the VPS29 L152E mutant [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.201797128" pmid="29158324" pmcid="PMC5770787" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>RAB7 is dysregulated in VPS35 KO cell lines and accumulates on endo-lysosomal membranes [<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38719-8" pmid="37248224" pmcid="PMC10227043" count="1">90</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Disruption of TBC1D5 interactions with RAB7 and the VPS35 leads to presynaptic excessive satellite boutons and branch formation, which phenocopies the loss of TBC1D5 [<citation rid="CR239" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jgg.2022.11.009" pmid="36473687" count="1">239</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additionally, in cortical neurons expressing <italic toggle="yes">VPS35 p.D620N</italic>, p.D620N mutant VPS35 was found in spines ∼30% less frequently compared to wild-type VPS35 in VPS35 wild-type cortical neurons, and a reduced number of dendritic spines was detected [<citation rid="CR244" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddu582" pmid="25416282" count="1">244</citation>].

The retromer influences neuroexcitatory chemical synapses through synaptic receptor recycling. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> models underexpressing <italic toggle="yes">vps29</italic>, the ELS was dysfunctional with impairment of synaptic receptor recycling and neurotransmission [<citation rid="CR245" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.51977" pmcid="PMC7182434" pmid="32286230" count="1">245</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer cargo adaptor SNX27 binds PDZ sequences present on many types of receptors, including NMDA receptors (NMDARs), β2AR, and 5-hydroxytryptamine 4a receptors (5-HT<sub>4(a)</sub>Rs) [<citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.201004060" pmid="20733053" pmcid="PMC2928020" count="1">119</citation>, <citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb.3290" pmid="27595347" count="1">120</citation>, <citation rid="CR127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3117" pmid="23524343" pmcid="PMC3911880" count="1">127</citation>, <citation rid="CR246" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms4176" pmid="24458027" pmcid="PMC3921469" count="1">246</citation>-<citation rid="CR249" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2014.02.018" pmid="24698268" pmcid="PMC4029335" count="1">249</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast to prior evidence, Clairfeuille et al. demonstrated that SNX27 does not directly bind the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor <bold>(</bold>AMPAR) [<citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb.3290" pmid="27595347" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Instead, SNX27 associates with the carboxy-terminal PDZ binding motif of the leucine-rich repeat and fibronectin type-III domain containing protein 2 (LRF2), whose N-terminal region binds AMPAR and regulates AMPAR sorting to the plasma membrane [<citation rid="CR250" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.59432" pmcid="PMC8296521" pmid="34251337" count="1">250</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27 also mediates endosome-to-plasma membrane trafficking of β2AR (Fig. 5) [<citation rid="CR251" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb2252" pmid="21602791" pmcid="PMC3113693" count="1">251</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Considering the role of SNX27 in the trafficking of retromer cargoes from the endosome to the plasma membrane, it can be postulated that it is through SNX27 that the retromer plays a part in regulating synaptic receptor recycling. <sentence_start/>In DS, chromosome 21 trisomy drives overexpression of miR-155, which leads to decreased <italic toggle="yes">SNX27</italic> expression. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">SNX27</italic> loss, in turn, leads to NMDA and AMPA receptor dysfunction associated with DS. <sentence_start/>Importantly, mouse models suggest that the synaptic and cognitive phenotypes associated with DS can be rescued through <italic toggle="yes">SNX27</italic> overexpression [<citation rid="CR127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3117" pmid="23524343" pmcid="PMC3911880" count="1">127</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Alzheimer’s disease:</italic> In AD, overactivation of NMDAR by glutamate is responsible for calcium-induced neuronal excitotoxicity and consequent loss of cholinergic neurons of the Nucleus basalis of Meynert, with consequent lower cerebral levels of Ach [<citation rid="CR252" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00401-015-1392-5" pmid="25633602" pmcid="PMC4366544" count="1">252</citation>, <citation rid="CR253" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms22094914" pmcid="PMC8124842" pmid="34066371" count="1">253</citation>]. <sentence_start/>NMDARs activity is modulated by AMPAR, which can increase or decrease NMDAR activity through sodium cascades or a calcium-calmodulin-dependent inactivation process [<citation rid="CR254" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.2002.020321" pmid="12181279" pmcid="PMC2290479" count="1">254</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In AD patients, there is a decrease in AMPA receptor levels and increased AMPA ubiquitination, with consequent neuronal internalization and proteasomal degradation [<citation rid="CR255" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JAD-170879" pmid="29614651" pmcid="PMC6353779" count="1">255</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The VPS26b and VPS35 modulate the activity and normal neuronal distribution and trafficking of AMPA receptors, controlling long-term potentiation (LTP), the neurobiological process of memory and learning (Fig. 6) [<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110182" pmid="34965419" pmcid="PMC8792909" count="1">94</citation>, <citation rid="CR249" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2014.02.018" pmid="24698268" pmcid="PMC4029335" count="1">249</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS26b and VPS35 deficiency lead to decreased dendritic spines and reduced GluA1 levels in hippocampal neurons and LTP dysfunction in mice [<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110182" pmid="34965419" pmcid="PMC8792909" count="1">94</citation>, <citation rid="CR147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110262" pmid="35045281" pmcid="PMC8830374" count="1">147</citation>, <citation rid="CR256" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2017.03.020" pmid="28384478" count="1">256</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the 5xFAD mice model of AD, transcranial injection of the retromer enhancer R55 ameliorates synaptic and LTP dysfunction observed in 5xFAD mice [<citation rid="CR257" ref-type="bibr" count="1">257</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Parkinson’s disease:</italic> In PD, dopamine receptor D1 (DRD1) and dopamine transporter (DAT) levels are decreased on the synaptic membrane, their trafficking is dysregulated and less DA reuptake results in increased DA metabolite production, such as DOPAC, with consequent oxidative stress and neurodegeneration [<citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2015.08.001" pmid="26321632" pmcid="PMC4565770" count="1">137</citation>, <citation rid="CR258" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2016.05.016" pmid="27460146" pmcid="PMC5018432" count="1">258</citation>-<citation rid="CR260" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrn983" pmid="12461550" count="1">260</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 favors DRD1 and DAT recycling to the cell surface, and activation of DRD downstream pathways, as evidenced by phosphorylation of the DA signaling effectors ERK and CREB (Fig. 8) [<citation rid="CR258" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2016.05.016" pmid="27460146" pmcid="PMC5018432" count="1">258</citation>, <citation rid="CR261" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3885-16.2017" pmid="28847807" pmcid="PMC5618262" count="1">261</citation>].

Retromer role in neurotransmission in Parkinson’s disease. <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Retromer’s role at the synaptic junction: (i) Vesicular Monoamine Transporter 2 (VMAT2) is a retromer cargo to the pre-synaptic endosomes; (ii) VPS35<sup>D620N</sup> neurons reveal re-distribution of Glutamate Receptor Subunit A1 (GluA1, or GluR1), with significantly increased GluR1 cluster intensity, indicating a role for the retromer in GluR1 trafficking between pre-synaptic endosomes and plasma membrane. <sentence_start/>Glutamatergic synapses on dopaminergic neurons regulate dopamine release via GluR1; (iii) retromer controls Dopamine Transporter (DAT) and (iv) Beta-2 Adrenergic Receptor (β2AR) recycling to the post-synaptic plasma membrane. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) At the neuronal cell body, the retromer regulates surface levels of Dopamine Receptor D1 (DRD1) and phosphorylation of the dopamine signaling effectors CREB and ERK. <sentence_start/>(C) The D620N mutated form of VPS35 is associated with (i) decreased VPS35 protein levels and impaired dendritic spine maturation with a reduced number of dendritic spines, (ii) localization in dendritic spines ∼30% less frequently compared to its wild-type form. <sentence_start/>Created in

VPS35 regulates DAT function and striatal DA transmission by functional interaction with LRRK2 [<citation rid="CR262" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41531-023-00609-7" pmid="38110354" pmcid="PMC10728137" count="1">262</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 could directly interact with LRRK2, as demonstrated by one study revealing LRRK2 and VPS35 co-immunoprecipitation [<citation rid="CR99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/BCJ20180248" pmid="29743203" pmcid="PMC5989534" count="1">99</citation>], though this was not observed in other studies [<citation rid="CR242" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddx179" pmid="28482024" count="1">242</citation>, <citation rid="CR263" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1318306111" pmid="24510904" pmcid="PMC3932908" count="1">263</citation>, <citation rid="CR264" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/mcp.M110.001172" pmcid="PMC3013447" pmid="20876399" count="1">264</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Overall, the mechanisms through which VPS35 modulates levels are decreased in PD and are associated with nigrostriatal dopamine dysfunction, resulting in neurodegeneration [<citation rid="CR265" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0319-07.2007" <sentence_start/>VMAT is a retromer cargo protein via VPS35 interaction (Fig. 8) [<citation rid="CR267" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7555/JBR.30.20160061" pmid="27924069" pmcid="PMC5138583" count="1">267</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Retromer enhancement increases VMAT2 levels in pre-clinical models of PD [<citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000204465" count="1">158</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, this therapeutic approach could play a role in regularizing dopaminergic neurotransmission in PD via restoring VMAT2 reserves.

Additionally, in PD, GluR1 (also known as GluA1) trafficking is altered, and VPS35 favors appropriate GluR1 re-distribution (Fig. 8) [<citation rid="CR244" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddu582" pmid="25416282" count="1">244</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Given that glutamatergic signaling stimulates DA release from SN, VPS35 indirectly favors appropriate dopaminergic neurotransmission in PD via GluR1 modulation [<citation rid="CR244" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddu582" pmid="25416282" count="1">244</citation>].

Recent evidence highlights the role of adrenergic receptor blockers as among the strongest independent factors for an older age of onset of PD [<citation rid="CR268" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00415-025-12989-2" pmid="40047945" pmcid="PMC11885381" count="1">268</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, other data suggest that beta blockers may be associated with an increased risk of developing PD [<citation rid="CR269" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.arr.2022.101670" pmid="35718329" count="1">269</citation>, <citation rid="CR270" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jns.2021.120009" pmid="34598055" count="1">270</citation>], although these data are controversial [<citation rid="CR271" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphar.2023.1107248" pmid="36909159" pmcid="PMC9995445" count="1">271</citation>, <citation rid="CR272" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s40263-020-00736-2" pmid="32500347" count="1">272</citation>]. <sentence_start/>SNX27 controls the downregulation and recycling to the cell surface of β2AR (Figs. 5 and 8) [<citation rid="CR251" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb2252" pmid="21602791" pmcid="PMC3113693" count="1">251</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These early findings highlight a potential new avenue of PD research, in which the retromer-mediated impact on βAR recycling and noradrenergic transmission may play a role in PD age of onset and progression.

In ALS, reduced levels of AMPA subunit GluA1 have been detected, and retromer involvement in AMPAR recycling in motor neurons is supported by early evidence, though yet to be demonstrated in detail (Fig. 4) [<citation rid="CR102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2118755119" pmid="35749364" pmcid="PMC9245686" count="1">102</citation>].

neurons and glial cells and play a role in intercellular communication in the CNS (Fig. 6) [<citation rid="CR273" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnmol.2022.844194" pmid="35493327" pmcid="PMC9043804" count="1">273</citation>]. <sentence_start/>NEVs also carry biomolecules for degradation, including misfolded forms of proteins involved in neurodegenerative diseases [<citation rid="CR274" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cells10050993" pmcid="PMC8146429" pmid="33922642" count="1">274</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In AD, increased APP is released extra-cellularly by neurons and spread through neuronal extracellular vesicles (NEVs) [<citation rid="CR241" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.202012034" pmcid="PMC8144913" pmid="34019080" count="1">241</citation>, <citation rid="CR273" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnmol.2022.844194" pmid="35493327" pmcid="PMC9043804" count="1">273</citation>-<citation rid="CR275" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-019-0317-5" pmid="31182115" pmcid="PMC6558712" count="1">275</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Early evidence reveals a role for Vps35 as an upstream regulator of NEV trafficking between neurons and APP delivery to synaptic NEVs in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic> models [<citation rid="CR241" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.202012034" pmcid="PMC8144913" pmid="34019080" count="1">241</citation>]. <sentence_start/>APP is required in both pre and post-synaptic terminals to regulate synaptic function and structure, highlighting how an appropriate APP localization and trafficking are relevant for synaptic physiology [<citation rid="CR276" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1750-1326-7-S1-L7" count="1">276</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, Vps35 may regulate synaptic function via APP trafficking through NEVs, though this has yet to be demonstrated.

Lysosomal exocytosis represents an additional mechanism for extracellular release of pathogenic proteins, including αS, potentially contributing to disease propagation [<citation rid="CR277" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-022-32625-1" pmid="35995799" pmcid="PMC9395532" count="1">277</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This has been noted in the context of dysfunctional lysosomes in Tg-αS<sup>A53T</sup>/CSPα<sup>−/−</sup> mice [<citation rid="CR277" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-022-32625-1" pmid="35995799" pmcid="PMC9395532" count="1">277</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the role of the retromer complex in this mechanism remains to be established.
Neuroinflammation via monocyte and microglia regulation is an additional pathogenetic process in neurodegenerative diseases controlled by the retromer (Table 1).

9). <sentence_start/>DAM can contain Aβ plaques and protect surrounding neuronal tissue (Fig. 9) [<citation rid="CR278" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41582-018-0072-1" pmid="30266932" count="1">278</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Microglial VPS35 is necessary in DAM development and Aβ uptake [<citation rid="CR279" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12974-022-02422-0" pmcid="PMC8892702" pmid="35236374" count="1">279</citation>, <citation rid="CR280" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature11729" pmid="23254930" pmcid="PMC3812809" count="1">280</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, count="1">281</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The retromer enhancer R55 favors a DAM and M2 anti-inflammatory microglia profile in response to the neuroinflammatory state in the AD microenvironment [<citation rid="CR257" ref-type="bibr" count="1">257</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 favors Aβ phagocytosis, a DAM and anti-inflammatory profile via recycling TREM2 (triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells) back to the plasma membrane (Fig. 9) [<citation rid="CR282" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/tra.12451" pmid="27717139" count="1">282</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In fact, microglia [<citation rid="CR282" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/tra.12451" pmid="27717139" count="1">282</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As mentioned above, microglial VPS35 also regulates microglial Aβ uptake [<citation rid="CR279" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12974-022-02422-0" pmcid="PMC8892702" pmid="35236374" count="1">279</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35 and TREM2 recruitment to the phagosomal membranes is regulated by beclin-1 (Fig. 9) [<citation rid="CR281" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2013.06.046" pmid="24012002" pmcid="PMC3779465" count="1">281</citation>].

Apolipoprotein E (APOE) is predominantly expressed by microglia and astrocytes [<citation rid="CR283" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/glia.23974" pmid="33556209" pmcid="PMC8717762" count="1">283</citation>] and remains the strongest and most prevalent genetic factor for sporadic AD, impacting more than half of all AD cases [<citation rid="CR284" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-022-00574-4" pmcid="PMC9644639" pmid="36348357" count="1">284</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Pathogenically, apoE seeds Aβ plaques in the brain, with the isoform apoE4 driving earlier and more abundant amyloids [<citation rid="CR284" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-022-00574-4" pmcid="PMC9644639" pmid="36348357" count="1">284</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Qureshi et al. demonstrated that APOE levels are increased in a genetic mouse model where VPS35 is depleted in hippocampal neurons, and partially normalized by VPS35 overexpression [<citation rid="CR147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110262" pmid="35045281" pmcid="PMC8830374" count="1">147</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, additional studies are necessary to further investigate retromer-mediated APOE regulation.

doi="10.4049/jimmunol.2100035" pmid="34507948" pmcid="PMC8490941" count="1">286</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Microglial NLRP3 activation is associated with dopaminergic neuronal loss and PD motor The retromer as a potential therapeutic target

The retromer’s key role in regulating multiple ELS-dependent mechanisms linked to neurodegeneration highlights its potential as a common therapeutic target across different neurodegenerative diseases. <sentence_start/>In vitro and in vivo studies implementing pharmacological enhancers of the retromer were originally conducted in AD models and revealed rescue from AD phenotypes [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These enhancers, TPT-260 (R55), and TPT-172 (R33) are part of the “R-compounds” drug class and were originally introduced by Mecozzi et al. in their seminal 2014 paper [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the VPS35, VPS26, VPS29 heterotrimer, VPS35 is the least stable subunit with a denaturation temperature of 38.5 °C, compared to 56.4 °C for VPS26 and 50 °C for VPS29 [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The addition of VPS26 to VPS35 results in a melting temperature of the complex of 53.4 °C, whereas the VPS35-VPS29 and VPS35-VPS29-VPS26 complex denatures closer to the temperature of Vps35 alone (45.5 °C) [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>After implementing two computational approaches and in silico screening of 46,000 compounds, only 4 docking sites on the VPS35-VPS29 interface were identified for secondary in vitro screening. <sentence_start/>Of the 24 compounds tested, only one, thiophene-2,5-diylbis(methylene) dicarbamimidothioate dihydrochloride (R55), improved the thermal stability of the core retromer protein complex by 10 °C at the highest concentration tested [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>R55 is predicted to make interactions with side chains from VPS35 and VPS29 [<citation rid="CR290" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13311-014-0321-y" pmid="25472693" pmcid="PMC4322078" count="1">290</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To identify the R55 binding site, mutagenesis experiments identified the Q538W mutation in VPS35 as preventing R55 from binding [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Further studies have shown that the R55 best docking site is a small surface recess surrounded by the Phe541 residue in VPS35, and by Tyr139 and Thr144 residues in VPS29 [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. <sentence_start/>R55 doses ranging from 0.5 µM to 50 µM were nontoxic to neurons [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Also, VPS35 protein, though not mRNA, levels were increased in neurons manipulated with R55, indicating protein stabilization without an effect on mRNA [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the same study, R33 (or thiophen-2-ylmethyl carbamimidothioate hydrochloride) was investigated and revealed the ability to bind the same pocket of R55, though with reduced potency, as demonstrated by an increase in VPS35 levels that was lower in magnitude compared to the levels observed for R55 [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>R55 was able to reduce the pathogenic processing of APP and Aβ levels in primary cultures of hippocampal neurons [<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.1508" pmid="24747528" pmcid="PMC4076047" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>hiPSC-derived neurons engineered with CRISPR/Cas9 to <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic> KO and APP Swedish mutation cells were treated with R33, showing its effectiveness in reducing Aβ and p-tau levels [<citation rid="CR291" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.stemcr.2018.01.031" pmcid="PMC5919412" pmid="29503090" count="1">291</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Last but not least, the chronic administration of R33 has been shown to improve memory and synaptic integrity, lower Aβ levels and deposition, and decrease tau pathology and neuroinflammation in a transgenic mouse model of AD [<citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-019-0350-4" pmid="31964406" pmcid="PMC6975032" count="1">152</citation>].

An additional retromer-interacting compound, 2a, was identified in 2020 by Muzio et al. [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. <sentence_start/>2a was modeled after R55, replacing the 2,5-disubstituted thiophene scaffold in R55 with a phenyl ring for synthetic versatility purposes and isothioureas with guanylhydrazones, as the latter show good stability and a pKa range closer to neutrality that promotes higher permeability through lipophilic bio-membranes and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. <sentence_start/>2a had significantly higher affinity than R55 for the same R55 binding site (Kd = 1.8 µM and Kd = 128.5 µM, respectively) [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, via X-ray diffraction experiments, the crystal structure of compound 2a bound to the VPS35-VPS29 complex has been resolved, identifying two novel binding sites beyond the known R55 binding site, providing structural evidence of target engagement with the retromer complex [<citation rid="CR165" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.csbj.2024.02.026" pmid="38487369" pmcid="PMC10937258" count="1">165</citation>]. <sentence_start/>VPS35, VPS26b and VPS29 proteins were significantly increased by compound 2a in Neuro2a cells after treatment for 48 h [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>]. 2a has been demonstrated to cross the BBB in wild type mice and the SOD1<sup>G93A</sup> mouse model of ALS, increasing retromer subunit protein levels, CI-MPR and mature form of the lysosomal hydrolase CTSD levels, decreasing misfolded SOD1 protein levels and rescuing the degeneration of MNs and motor defects [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>].

More recent data on the effect of 2a in PD have been investigated by our group [<citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>, <citation rid="CR292" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2019.01272" pmid="31920908" pmcid="PMC6928206" count="1">292</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Administration of 2a in a PD mouse model increased VPS35 protein levels, retromer cargo proteins, and the mature form of the lysosomal hydrolase CTSD, supporting an enhancement of retromer functional activity [<citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This was associated with decreased oligomeric αS levels and protection against degeneration of SN dopaminergic neurons, highlighting a disease-modifying function [<citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Challenges in targeting the retromer complex:</italic> One important challenge in targeting the retromer therapeutically is maintaining the stoichiometric balance among its subunits. <sentence_start/>The retromer functions as a tightly regulated multimeric complex whose subunits exist in equilibrium with each other. <sentence_start/>This is demonstrated by the ability of the subunits to form higher-order oligomeric arrangements of the retromer at higher subunit concentrations [<citation rid="CR188" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0854.2010.01124.x" pmid="20875039" count="1">188</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additionally, VPS26 depletion also decreased the levels of VPS29 and VPS35 [<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2021.110182" pmid="34965419" pmcid="PMC8792909" count="1">94</citation>, <citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0802545105" pmid="18480253" pmcid="PMC2386077" count="1">96</citation>, <citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.200312055" pmid="15078903" pmcid="PMC2172094" count="1">104</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, a stoichiometric imbalance between the retromer subunits could alter the retromer assembly process and function. <sentence_start/>These observations suggest that selectively increasing a single retromer subunit level or function may not be sufficient and could even disrupt retromer homeostasis. <sentence_start/>As such, pharmacological strategies should aim to stabilize or enhance the function of the assembled retromer complex rather than disproportionately increasing individual subunits. <sentence_start/>Small molecules acting as pharmacological chaperones that promote coordinated stabilization of the VPS35-VPS29-VPS26 complex may represent a more balanced and physiologically relevant therapeutic approach. <sentence_start/>This small-molecule approach may also offer an advantage over retromer genetic overexpression strategies, as it is intended to enhance endogenous retromer function rather than induce supraphysiological increases in individual subunits. 2a increases the levels of all the subunits of the retromer (VPS35, VPS26b and VPS29) [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>], and further studies are currently undergoing to investigate the details of this mechanistic effect on the retromer.

Second, given the retromer’s involvement in different cellular pathways, the enhancement of its function may alter cellular homeostasis and trigger unintended downstream effects. <sentence_start/>In fact, a potential caveat to retromer enhancement implementation in neurodegenerative disease clinical practice is its impact on different cancer hallmarks. <sentence_start/>In pre-clinical models of gastric carcinomas, VPS35 promotes tumor growth, invasion, and metastasis via integrin-mediated activation of FAK-SRC kinases [<citation rid="CR293" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-023-02885-2" pmid="37950040" pmcid="PMC10774127" count="1">293</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the same model, VPS35 knockdown increased the sensitivity of cancer cells to 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin, highlighting VPS35’s role in chemoresistance and cancer progression [<citation rid="CR293" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-023-02885-2" pmid="37950040" pmcid="PMC10774127" count="1">293</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additional pre-clinical evidence has been demonstrated in other cancer types, among which are hepatocellular and cervical carcinoma, with data revealing VPS35’s role in cancer cell proliferation, invasion, apoptosis and metastasis, genomic instability, and immune evasion of cancer [<citation rid="CR294" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13578-021-00585-6" pmid="33858520" pmcid="PMC8048225" count="1">294</citation>-<citation rid="CR296" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adp4917" pmid="39413192" pmcid="PMC11482321" count="1">296</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, it remains unclear whether VPS35 mutations act as oncogenic drivers, with evidence limited to neural progenitor-derived cells in <italic toggle="yes">Drosophila</italic>, highlighting the retromer as a safeguard mechanism against Notch-mediated brain tumor formation [<citation rid="CR297" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.38181" pmcid="PMC6140715" pmid="30176986" count="1">297</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As such, retromer function enhancement via R-compounds or retromer overexpression carries a risk of side effects in patients. <sentence_start/>This aspect will need to be considered for potential future clinical trials investigating the safety and efficacy of retromer stabilizers in AD, PD and ALS patients. <sentence_start/>A potential approach could be excluding from the trial any patient with a past medical history of malignancy.

To mitigate these potential risks, ongoing preclinical studies are designed to comprehensively characterize the on-target and off-target effects of retromer-stabilizing small molecules before clinical translation. <sentence_start/>These studies include mechanistic analyses to define how the pharmacological approach modulates retromer complex activity and the ELS, together with IND-enabling safety assessments, including mutagenicity, genotoxicity, toxicology, and pharmacokinetic profiling, including its plasma and brain concentration, tissue distribution, and BBB penetration. <sentence_start/>Together, these studies will help define a therapeutic window in which retromer activity can be enhanced while minimizing the risk of perturbing cellular homeostasis, promoting unwanted proliferative pathways, or inducing long-term toxic effects.

AD, PD, and ALS are neurodegenerative diseases related to each other by similar pathogenetic mechanisms. <sentence_start/>A central mechanism is the presence of a dysfunctional ELS, which affects four common pathways in AD, PD and ALS. <sentence_start/>Impaired ELS-regulated proteostasis leads to misfolded proteins, whose accumulation and aggregation likely contribute to neuronal injury and death. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the ELS is involved in mitochondrial biogenesis and homeostasis dysfunction, with abnormal mitochondrial fragmentation and increased oxidative stress and cellular apoptosis. <sentence_start/>Deficits in neurotransmitter reuptake and synaptic receptor recycling and clearance are also important. <sentence_start/>Neuroinflammation is an additional mechanism affected by ELS dysfunction. <sentence_start/>The retromer is at the cornerstone of each one of these processes, modulating the ELS and rescuing the above-mentioned interconnected processes in diseased neurons and reactive microglia. <sentence_start/>A relatively novel class of molecular chaperones, enhancers of the retromer, has proven to slow the neurodegenerative phenotype typical of PD and ALS in in vitro and in vivo models [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-17524-7" pmid="32737286" pmcid="PMC7395176" count="1">103</citation>, <citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-019-0350-4" pmid="31964406" pmcid="PMC6975032" count="1">152</citation>, <citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" count="1">155</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Retromer stabilization’s neuroprotective effect lies in favoring the ELS homeostasis with trafficking of lysosomal hydrolases and cargo receptors, facilitating the degradation of amyloidogenic proteins such as Aβ and αS, as well as misfolded proteins including SOD1 and TDP-43. <sentence_start/>Beyond its role in protein clearance, retromer stabilization has been shown to dampen neuroinflammation and facilitate neurotransmission. <sentence_start/>As such, retromer enhancement represents a multifaceted therapeutic strategy leading to neuroprotection across different neurodegenerative disorders. <sentence_start/>This preclinical evidence highlights the role of retromer enhancers as potential drugs that could step into clinical trials for multiple neurodegenerative conditions.
